💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architecture studio SIGNIFICANT has unveiled looks for Refugee City, a masterplan that reimagines the Bidi Bidi refugee settlement in Uganda as an economic hub.
  • Developed by SIGNIFICANT in collaboration with social enterprise To.org, the masterplan proposes essential civic infrastructure such as housing, schools and markets for the largest refugee settlement in Africa, home to around 250,000 displaced people.
  • The initiative was conceptualised as an alternative to short-term aid and charity-led approaches to refugee settlements, providing a “resilient economic model” that empowers displaced communities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Architecture studio SIGNIFICANT has unveiled looks for Refugee City, a masterplan that reimagines the Bidi Bidi refugee settlement in Uganda as an economic hub.

Developed by SIGNIFICANT in collaboration with social enterprise To.org, the masterplan proposes essential civic infrastructure such as housing, schools and markets for the largest refugee settlement in Africa, home to around 250,000 displaced people.

The initiative was conceptualised as an alternative to short-term aid and charity-led approaches to refugee settlements, providing a “resilient economic model” that empowers displaced communities.

“If the average stay in refugee camps is around two decades, then the term temporary cannot be remarked to suffice,” said studio founder Bjarke Ingels.

“If we start thinking of cities rather than camps, then charity becomes investments into the future, and if companies can be incentivised to locate their production in refugee cities, then the refugees can be given economic opportunities that they currently long for.”.

If completed, the project would sit alongside an existing performing arts centre completed on the site in 2024.

The masterplan is designed by SUBSTANTIAL to be “scalable and modular” to facilitate its implementation in other locations.

“We have attempted to design a scalable, phaseable, modular blueprint for a latest way to accommodate the global flow of refugees,” Ingels stated.

In a bid to allow the city to grow organically, the proposal takes a “fractal approach” – beginning with the establishment of housing units before expanding to neighbourhoods and eventually districts over several years.

The first phase of the project comprises a prototype single-family housing unit, which is currently being built on the site. Its modular structure was designed to improve existing shelter typologies, while also drawing on local buildings.

Once complete, the unit will function as an operational guesthouse to accommodate international investors and future collaborators on the site.

“The prototype base unit is inspired by local vernacular settlements where homes grow as a sequence of rooms around shared spaces,” To.org co-founder Nachson Mimran told Dezeen.

Renders of the city reveal designs for a commercial street lined with markets and built from local materials such as brick and bamboo.

The Bidi Bidi settlement in Uganda was chosen as the site for the inaugural Refugee City because of the country’s 2006 Refugee Act, which grants refugees the right to work and start businesses, freedom of movement, and to acquire agricultural plots within integrated rural settlements.

“There are very few nations offering this unique combination which makes Uganda the ideal location for the inaugural Refugee City,” Mimran said.

The realisation of the full-scale masterplan in Bidi Bidi is dependent on capital investment, while any future initiatives will require host-nation governments to be willing to grant flexibility and legal work rights to refugees.

Other spaces designed for refugees include an easy-build playground for children fleeing war, and wooden refugee beds designed to provide more privacy and dignity.

According to recent reports, if you're even more into video, the R6 V is an interesting option. It borrows heavily from the Canon EOS R6 III, which is a great hybrid camera, and tilts everything a bit more toward video workflows. We really like it.

The 45-megapixel Canon EOS R5 II is probably Canon's best mirrorless camera overall. It combines resolution and speed and captures great video to boot. It's an excellent camera and one that many different types of enthusiasts and professionals can use to great effect. It's $3,999 right now after $400 in instant savings.

The Canon PowerShot V1 is an all-in-one camera with a 22.3-megapixel Type 1.4 image sensor and 16-50mm-equivalent f/2.8-4.5 lens. It has a built-in ND filter, captures 4Kp60 video, and shoots photos at up to 30 frames per second. PetaPixel declared, "PowerShot is back," when we reviewed the camera last year. It's $849 thanks to a $180 discount.

Industry observers note that the Canon RF 24-70mm f/2.8L IS USM is a workhorse lens for many photographers and videographers. It's pricey, but a $200 discount helps a bit. It's $2,399 right now.

In a recent development, another go-to zoom for pros is the original RF 70-200mm f/2.8L IS USM (not the newer "Z" version). Unlike the Z lens, this model employs a telescoping design, allowing it to collapse into a much more compact size. It's $2,699 after a $300 discount.

On the complete opposite end of the price scale is the RF 50mm f/1.8 STM, the "nifty fifty." It's a great lens for a lot of photographers, especially those looking for something faster than their kit zoom. It's $199 thanks to a $40 discount.

This doesn't fit nicely into any other category above, but the Canon IVY 2 Mini Photo Printer is $20 off, bringing it to $99. It prints pocket-sized photo stickers and works alongside your smartphone. It uses ZINK ("Zero Ink") technology. I actually own one of these and use it to make fun gifts for people, and it's a blast.

Sources indicate that for those who want really good print quality and big prints, the Canon imagePROGRAF PRO-1100 is a professional-grade 17-inch-wide printer that delivers fantastic results. It is $254 off until the end of the day on November 14, which brings its price down to $1,149.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that shanghai’s two leading art fairs, West Bund Art & Design and Art021, opened this week against a backdrop of slowing economic growth, subdued confidence in China’s art market and an increasingly crowded international art calendar. While the city no longer commands the same international panache it enjoyed before the pandemic, galleries report encouraging early sales, suggesting that committed collectors remain active despite a more cautious market.

Industry observers note that “I think the serious people who have a long-term idea of what they want to do, they keep collecting,” says René Meile, director of Galerie Urs Meile, which has a location in Beijing. He adds that younger collectors increasingly favour artists of their own generation. While established artists continued to attract buyers, collectors were taking longer to commit to expensive works. Meile attributed the shift partly to the departure of speculative buyers from the market.

Industry observers note that meanwhile this year’s art week brings an explosion of art events city-wide and boasts many newcomers both in terms of industry visitors and fresh spaces, including three new galleries. Hangzhou’s longtime fair regular Inna Art Space just opened Inna Front Room in the Lujiazui business district, making it the first significant gallery on the Pudong side of the river. Chen Yongwei, the former director of nonprofit Pond Society, has opened Shanghai Industry atop the Suhe House art cluster. PTT Space, a rising star gallery from Taipei, meanwhile this week opened an outpost at the M50 gallery complex.

“Even though the Chinese market is at an all-time low, Shanghai is still a vibrant international city with many art institutions,” says Robert Hsu, who founded PTT in 2020. “Considering the past art week, the number of openings parties and fairs is still through the roof, surpassing Seoul Art Week and coming close to Hong Kong Art Week.”.

According to recent reports, hsu indicates he also has existing “base infrastructure” in the city with staff and relationships with local artists and collectors. “As a second generation gallerist, I feel we have to keep moving in this new era. The market, the business, the people have all changed. To survive, I have to step out of our comfort zone and explore.”.

Jae Pil Eun's Night Walking, showing at Hang Over.

Courtesy of the artists and SYSTEMA © SYSTEMA, 2026.

Along with the gallery, Hsu is part of the team organising the newly introduced boutique fair Art Fusion Canton in the southern Chinese city Guangzhou next month (3-7 December). In Shanghai, the popup fair Hang Over (11-15 November) is going strong in its second year. Moving from last year’s restaurant to an event space in a new lifestyle complex on Donghu Lu, it this year features 18 galleries including Tokyo’s Misako & Rosen, Seoul’s Cylinder along with Shanghai’s Antenna Space, Vanguard and Linseed, owned by Hang Over founder Zhuang Lingzhi.

The 13th edition of West Bund Art & Design (10–15 November) brought together 85 galleries, including Hauser & Wirth, Perrotin, Thaddaeus Ropac and White Cube. Meanwhile, the 14th Art021, hosting 111 galleries at the Shanghai Exhibition Centre, has introduced a newly introduced acquisition initiative with the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (Lacma), supported by Chinese collectors, aimed at bringing works by Asian and Asian diaspora artists into the museum’s collection.

It has been revealed that at West Bund, Thaddaeus Ropac reports several opening-day sales, led by Megan Rooney’s That Sky (Atlas) (2026), sold for £400,000 to a Chinese foundation. Other transactions included a painting by Martha Jungwirth for €200,000, a Robert Longo work for $90,000 and a painting by Han Bing for €55,000, acquired by an Asian museum. A work by Joan Snyder was also sold to a Chinese museum.

Visitor at West Bund Art & Design 2026.

Courtesy of West Bund Art & Design.

It has been revealed that dawn Zhu, the gallery’s Asia director, praises the enthusiasm of collectors, noting that the gallery had made early sales to both institutions and private collections. “We are seeing collectors who have travelled from across South East Asia and even a few from Europe,” she notes.

Hauser & Wirth also reports significant sales at West Bund, led by Louise Bourgeois’s bronze sculpture Point of Contact (1967–68, cast 2006), which sold for $450,000 to a museum in Kuala Lumpur. Other transactions include Lee Bul’s Perdu XXXIII (2020), sold for $260,000 to a private collection in China, and another Bourgeois work, Femme (2008), acquired by a Chinese private collector for $165,000. The gallery also reports the sale of George Condo’s Black and Red Composition (2026) for $200,000.

At Art021, Galerie Urs Meile reports sales of works by Xie Nanxing for approximately RMB 1.2m and Ju Ting for RMB 400,000, alongside works by younger artists Chen Zuo and Miao Miao priced between RMB 100,000 and RMB 150,000, and a smaller painting by Vietnamese artist Mai Ta for RMB 40,000.

Also at Art021, Shanghai-based gallery Bank reports strong early sales of Liang Hao’s works, priced 60,000 to 300,000 RMB, and of a large Jiang Cheng painting for over 500,000 RMB. The gallery reports that Lacma may acquire a video work made in 2000 by Los Angeles-based artist Patty Chang.

It has been revealed that despite the more subdued atmosphere, some galleries remain optimistic about the depth of China’s domestic market. Liang Xiao, a spokesperson for Perrotin, which has operated a Shanghai space since 2018, indicates that the slowdown had given collectors more time to select works they genuinely appreciate.

Sources indicate that he suggests that the growth of new art fairs in Yokohama, Seoul and elsewhere would not fundamentally undermine Shanghai’s position, given the size of China’s domestic collector base. “Even after all these years, there are still many collectors we have yet to reach,” Liang notes, adding that Shanghai remains an crucial entry point for collectors from across mainland China.

In a recent development, hsu notes the feedback for PTT Shanghai has been “quite positive” in the debut week, but “the market is not at its best.” Transactions have been slow, but included some successful placement of works with established collectors. “As the old saying goes, the gallery business is a marathon, not a sprint.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • is pleased to present The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins, Molly Bounds’ Newly introduced York debut solo exhibition, on view at the gallery’s 6040 56th Drive location.
  • Opening on the vernal equinox, a rare moment when the hours of daylight and night are equal, Molly Bounds offers light as the protagonist in her newly introduced series of paintings.
  • In a recent development, bounds captures her subjects in solitude.

Mrs. is pleased to present The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins, Molly Bounds’ Newly introduced York debut solo exhibition, on view at the gallery’s 6040 56th Drive location. This exhibition marks the Los Angeles-based artist’s second presentation with the gallery following The Armory Show in September 2025. The show will be on view through May 2, 2026.

Opening on the vernal equinox, a rare moment when the hours of daylight and night are equal, Molly Bounds offers light as the protagonist in her newly introduced series of paintings. It is versatile and ever-changing; it both conceals and reveals, and reminds us of the unrelenting forward movement of time. Depicting her subjects both in contemplation and in the midst of candid movement, Bounds continues her investigation into liminal moments where stillness and urgency shape the mood. Much like the transition from winter to spring, these figures appear on the threshold of a transformative shift.

In a recent development, bounds captures her subjects in solitude. Her interior scenes feature slumped and draping bodies signaling rest and repose that slowly gives way to unease. These are psychological portraits, capturing something that persists behind dormant states and tired eyes. In The Armchair, the warm glow of a fireplace highlights a textured and lush interior, contrasted against the cold, early evening blue sky seen out the window. Contemplation gradually reveals tension - a mind dwelling, scheming, planning; upholstery seams unravel. The woman maintains a vacant stare that lingers in an eternal way, in bliss or something else.In Privacy Glass, another figure secludes herself from the outside world, rendered dramatically in both warm and cool hues. The glass offers a clear diffusion to illuminate the subject from behind, while letting a distinct  beam permeate the inside from the outside. The result obscures her face and accents her draped clothing, recalling a Georges De La Tour: like the vanitas, Bounds conveys the fleetingness of time and inevitability of darkness.

In a recent development, there are also moments of escapism. In both It Sings in Me and Among of Green, Again a figure moves freely amongst rolling green hills, illuminated under the sun. The landscape appears bucolic and perhaps overly so - is this real or imagined? For Bounds this is less crucial; the ability to build optimism and a belief in renewal and rebirth is paramount. Contrasting with the scenes of pensive interiority, these landscapes communicate urgency, celebration, possibility, and fantasy. After the darkness of winter, spring wins.

Polestar Formula 2030 concept car "screams performance"

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Swedish electric-vehicle brand Polestar has unveiled the Formula 2030 concept car featuring interchangeable, customisable dashboard buttons.
  • The first Polestar concept created under the direction of head of design Philipp Römers, the Formula 2030 is intended to herald the design direction of the firm’s production cars in the coming years.
  • It takes the form of a low-slung sports car with proportions that Römers remarked “scream performance”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Swedish electric-vehicle brand Polestar has unveiled the Formula 2030 concept car featuring interchangeable, customisable dashboard buttons.

The first Polestar concept created under the direction of head of design Philipp Römers, the Formula 2030 is intended to herald the design direction of the firm’s production cars in the coming years.

It takes the form of a low-slung sports car with proportions that Römers remarked “scream performance”.

With signature “Dual Blade” headlights, the front of the car previews the face of the next-generation Polestar 2, a saloon scheduled to launch in 2027.

Meanwhile, the tail of the Formula 2030 mirrors the upcoming Polestar 7 crossover SUV, moving away from the continuous rear lightbar that has become widespread among electric cars in favour of separate “Single Blade” lights.

Unlike Polestar’s most recently released production vehicles, the Polestar 4 and Polestar 5, the Formula 2030 also has a conventional rear windscreen.

“Design should always reflect the values and mission of a brand and that is exactly what we did with Polestar Formula 2030 concept,” said Römers, who joined Polestar from Audi in January 2025.

“It is a physical embodiment of how we apply Polestar’s core values of design, performance and sustainability to the next production cars.”.

At 1.35 metres tall, 4.68 metres long and 2.02 metres wide, the Formula 2030 has a very low roofline but a broad stance.

Its styling was intended to project power, with a long bonnet, wraparound windscreen, short overhangs, muscular haunches and substantial 22-inch wheels.

Other sporty design elements include a deep front splitter and a single vertical windscreen wiper.

The Formula 2030 showcases a newly developed paint colour called Nitrogen, with accents of gold dotted throughout the car.

Inside, the design echoes efforts in recent concept cars from other carmakers to emphasise the driving experience.

The cockpit features a curved screen band mounted above the steering wheel, presenting information to the driver.

Another screen is integrated into the centre console, which slopes gently up to the dashboard.

A sliding “drive mode selector” on the centre console would allow the car to alternate between three modes – Performance, Normal and Autonomous – changing the angle of the central screen, seating and steering wheel to allow for a more passive or active driving position.

The Formula 2030 embraces a wider trend in car design back towards incorporating physical buttons, rather than only touchscreens.

According to recent reports, also occupying the central console is an interface of eight large mechanical controls. These can be configured to the user’s preferences, with choices between different types of buttons and switches capable of being programmed for specific functions.

In a modest nod to sustainability, the seat backs are made from a bio-based composite combining European flax and bio-based polypropylene, while the insides of the doors are made from a single material in order to be recyclable.

Headquartered in Gothenburg, Polestar has emphasised design and sustainability since it was spun out of Volvo as a premium EV brand in 2017.

It has been revealed that amid heavy financial losses, it has increased its production of SUVs, which tend to be popular with consumers and deliver higher profit margins. SUVs or SUV-adjacent cars now account for three of the five models in its lineup.

SUVs are often associated with a greater environmental impact than other types of cars, but Polestar denies watering down its ambitions on sustainability.

According to its most recent sustainability report, published in April, the company is ahead of schedule on a target to halve greenhouse-gas emissions per vehicle sold between 2020 and 2030.

It is the only car brand that publishes life-cycle carbon assessments for all its models. Assessments for the upcoming Polestar 2 and Polestar 7 have not yet been calculated.

“Learnings from the cars we have already produced will be channelled into the new cars to bring the CO2e figures in as low as possible,” a spokesperson told Dezeen.

In 2021, Polestar declared a project to produce a “truly climate-neutral car” by 2030. Earlier this year, it pushed this target back to 2035 owing to the “scale and complexity of the challenge”.

Other concept cars recently covered on Dezeen include the flying Tesla Roadster and a Fiat that transforms from an SUV into a pickup truck.

In the afterglow of the blue-nami, those of us who make, organize, fund, and sustain cultural life are feeling a twinge of hope. But I find myself slipping into a spiral of anxiety as the everyday reality of economic precarity sets back in. Our newly elected Democratic congressional leaders have an opportunity to change that reality — pushing back against Trump is necessary — but it cannot be the full extent of their ambition.

According to recent reports, as a curator and the co-director of an arts nonprofit, I’ve been asked what the results mean for the so-called “art world.” My first response was cynical: “not much.” At least not immediately. An election does not directly restore a canceled grant or pay an artist’s rent. And even a return to the funding landscape that existed before Trump took office in 2025 would leave us with a system that was already failing the people expected to sustain it.

Instead, the midterm election results should serve as an opening to hold Democrats in Congress accountable for making arts and cultural life materially sustainable, not simply to defend an inadequate system from further attack. That mandate concerns whose histories are told, who gets paid to make art, and who gets to define the country’s future. It also concerns whether the people doing that work can afford to keep going.

#74. Europol Warns of More Aggressive Museum Heists as Thieves Change Tactics and Targets

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (553 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Artnews

Europol Warns of More Aggressive Museum Heists as Thieves Change Tactics and Targets

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It seems like news of newly introduced museum robberies just keeps coming, particularly in the months following the brazen Louvre heist one year ago.
  • According to recent reports, what does Europol tell us?
  • The kinds of things getting stolen are also changing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It seems like news of newly introduced museum robberies just keeps coming, particularly in the months following the brazen Louvre heist one year ago. In an attempt to shed light on the phenomenon, Europol published a study in August, Changing Tactics, Changing Targets: The Evolving Nature of Museum Heists, which examines key trends within these more recent crimes, as reported earlier by The Art Newspaper.

According to recent reports, what does Europol tell us? For one, the old notion that museum thefts are generally non-violent, or use stealthy tactics such as replacing precious jewels or artworks with convincing fakes, is no longer the case. “Offenders are adopting more direct and confrontational approaches,” as well as “a growing use of force” to break into museums and display cases using tools like sledgehammers, axes, crowbars, and sometimes explosives, states the report. On some occasions, museum workers have been intimidated with weapons, but also directly assaulted. According to the report, Louvre staff and visitors were threatened by the men who broke into the museum during its opening hours on October 19, 2025, and successfully fled with over $102 million worth of the country’s crown jewels. Related Articles Suspected Thieves Flee Dresden Museum Complex After Being Spotted by Security Guard Louvre Heist Suspect Denied Release As Investigators Unravel Tangled Testimonies.

The kinds of things getting stolen are also changing. In the last few years, thieves have increasingly been going for precious stones and metals such as gold, which can be melted down, cut, or taken apart from their casings and sold without a trace. Plus, these materials attract attention due to a “perception that museum security measures are less robust than those in jewelry stores.”.

Chinese cultural artifacts have also become hot targets. These include examples such as 12th- and 13th-century porcelain jars and vases from the Ming Dynasty, plus colored enamels on bronze vases from both the Ming and Qing Dynasties. The report affirms these Chinese cultural goods are in high demand and “are likely to be easily sold on the art market.”.

As for the perpetrators, they tend to have a history of involvement with other types of crime, and increasingly, coordinate with accomplices on an “ad hoc basis,” or without prior connection. In other words, these are not necessarily organized networks built around a core group or leader. As a result, investigators have theorized that criminals may be randomly recruiting “low-level” accomplices or perpetrators to break into museums.

Sources indicate that as for the frequency of museum heists, the report does not mention whether they have gone up. Jean-Yves Goriou, head of the EU Organized Crime Unit in Europol’s European Serious and Organized Crime Centre (ESOCC), did confirm in an interview with TAN that, “We have observed a clear and steep increase in the number of museum robbery cases since around 2022/2023.”.

However, that view was contrasted with that of another expert, Robert Read, the head of art and private clients at Hiscox Insurance. “In the sense of volume of crimes [against museums], there’s not been a change,” he said. Meanwhile, Julian Radcliffe, the director of the Art Loss Register, observes that “A lot of these trends [in the Europol report] are not new, but they’re arguably occurring on a more pronounced or regular scale.” It sure feels that way.

#73. Samsung P9 SSD Review: Finally Best in Class

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1371 w)
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Petapixel

Samsung P9 SSD Review: Finally Best in Class

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1371 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I have been very hard on Samsung SSDs over the last few years.
  • Samsung has finally produced a slim, fast, and cost-effective portable SSD that is the best in its class.
  • In a recent development, prior to the P9, Samsung used USB 3.2 Gen 2×2, which can provide peak speeds of up to 2,000 MB/s… as long as you’re using the right connection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I have been very hard on Samsung SSDs over the last few years. The T-series SSDs have been hugely popular among photographers because of their compact size, but I have never liked them because of their atrocious transfer speeds. For what they cost, they just aren’t worth it. But Samsung finally has me changing my tune.

Samsung has finally produced a slim, fast, and cost-effective portable SSD that is the best in its class.

In a recent development, prior to the P9, Samsung used USB 3.2 Gen 2×2, which can provide peak speeds of up to 2,000 MB/s… as long as you’re using the right connection. Gen 2×2 has always been badly supported on all computers, but it is particularly badly supported on Apple devices, where a single Apple computer in the last decade supported it on just one of its USB ports.

Gen 2×2 was always meant as a stopgap between USB 3.2 and USB4, but manufacturers kept using it because it was cheaper than paying for the higher USB4 components, while it also let them claim super-high transfer speeds on the box. This was, for a majority of people, effectively a lie: most would never see anywhere near those speed promises and would instead cap out at sub-800 MB/s peak read and write speeds.

In a recent development, I was willing to forgive this back when the T7, T8, and T9 SSDs cost under $100, but these days the MSRP of these SSDs has ballooned to around or over $260 for 1TB and $1,000 for 4TB. That’s an insane price for such low performance, especially given the alternatives.

Industry observers note that what I can never fault Samsung for is its SSD design: small, thin, and light. The T series got this bang-on, and the latest P9 really does a good job with carrying that forward.

Recent findings suggest that samsung has slowly moved away from its rubber or silicone wrap that it put around the T7 as it evolved the series, and the latest T9 moved to a “carbon pattern” rubber that was significantly less thick. The P9 feels like the next logical step: fully moving away from that kind of a wrap and leaving the metal bare. This makes the design feel less rugged, but it is unlikely to make a major difference for most people in practice. Perhaps it won’t be quite as drop-resistant – and Samsung isn’t really talking about that at all, actually – but I personally prefer it. I just was not a fan of how the T series felt in hand.

Recent findings suggest that there is really not a lot else to talk about with the design of this little SSD. It has a single USB4 port, an indicator light, a little embossed line for design effect only, and Samsung’s logo. Simple, light, straightforward, and svelte.

Recent findings suggest that I will say that the corded USB cable that Samsung includes with the P9 is very nice and is a good length (about a foot long). It includes two Velcro cable ties to keep it organized in your tech bag, and it is wholly unbranded (which I also like).

If I had one knock on the P9 design, it’s that the all-metal exterior scuffs very easily. I put this P9 in my bag for one quick trip to Los Angeles earlier this month, and it has a pretty noticeable blemish now. People tend not to care about this too much, but if you’re someone who likes to keep their tech neat and clean, that might be hard with the P9.

As I mentioned before, Samsung SSDs have always had a nice design, but the performance was woefully lacking. That finally changes with the P9.

According to recent reports, as a recap, PetaPixel‘s storage testing involves speed testing SSDs brand-upcoming out of the box, filling the SSD to capacity and testing again, and then emptying the SSD and testing a third time. We also have recently added Amorphous DiskMark to our Blackmagic Speed Test bench, but we continue to use the Blackmagic numbers in our historical chart for the sake of consistency.

The SSD I tested is Samsung’s 2TB capacity option.

These are great numbers, especially compared to Samsung’s previously woeful performance with USB 3.2 Gen 2×2. They are not close to the best we’ve seen out of other USB4 SSDs or Thunderbolt 5, but they’re very good. The P9 has support for first-gen USB4, so it caps out at 40 Gbps and won’t match the speeds of the Oyen U35 Bolt+ or the Glyph EX80, but it does compete well against the ProGrade PG10 and the Glyph EX40.

Industry observers note that there is a dip in write performance when the SSD fills, which is worth noting, but its peaks are higher than both Glyph and ProGrade USB4 Gen 1 options. I think this matters even more when you consider the size and weight of the Samsung P9: it’s significantly smaller and lighter than other options in its tier. I could carry three P9s for around the same size and bulk as a single Glyph EX40, for example.

In use, the Samsung P9 is completely silent, which is expected given it has no moving parts, but it is also surprisingly good at sinking heat despite its thin and small chassis. It does get warm when under load, but that warmth doesn’t last for long and swiftly returns to below body temperature and feels cold to the touch. I didn’t see any evidence of thermal throttling either. Overall, fantastic performance.

Industry observers note that as often as I am hard on brands, I am willing to give praise when it is earned: Samsung has created an SSD that maintains all of the benefits of the T series while finally backing that up with performance. This is a fantastic little SSD that performs well. Somewhat surprisingly, it’s not crazy expensive either: $340 for 1TB. Compared to the $290 retail price of the Samsung T9 for the same capacity, it’s well worth it to jump over to USB4 for the $50 upcharge, as you’re getting way, way better speeds with the P9 versus the T9 (or T8 or T7).

This is still a worthwhile purchase even if you don’t have a USB4-compatible computer, since it’s better to invest in products that can grow with you rather than hold you back. The next time you get a computer, it’s more likely than not going to come equipped with USB4 support, and you will want to be able to take advantage of that instead of being left behind on USB 3.2.

As mentioned, the Samsung T series (most recently the T9) is going to be the most obvious direct competitor. It’s cheaper, but not by much and certainly not by enough to accept the huge dip in performance. The P9 is nearly five times faster than the T9 for an extra $50. To me, that’s a no-brainer.

The aforementioned Glyph EX40 is a direct USB4 (generation one) competitor, and it is significantly heavier and bigger and has worse performance in most circumstances. It is more consistent under heavy load, but many will see the much smaller P9 as a better choice to shed some weight. Additionally, the P9 is $100 cheaper than Glyph at the 1TB capacity. Both the EX40 and the P9 offer 2TB, 4TB, and 8TB options, and as the capacity goes up, Glyph’s price gets more competitive until it is actually cheaper at 8TB ($2,450 versus $2,700).

The ProGrade PG10 is in a class of its own since it is only available in the 16TB configuration right now, and if you need that much capacity, it is a more cost-effective option at $4,200 versus the $5,400 it would cost to buy two 8TB Samsung P9 SSDs. ProGrade’s PG10 is also slower, especially the 16TB version, which tested worse than ProGrade’s lower capacities it once offered.

Sources indicate that yes. Samsung has finally produced a slim, fast, and cost-effective portable SSD that is the best in its class.

  • Named Zando Central Market, the building replaces a historic market on the same site in Kinshasa that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Martin Argyroglo excluding top photo by Ville Kinshasa & SZTC.

French studio Think Tank Architecture has created a market in the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, with space for 20,000 vendors across its geometric brick-and-concrete structure.

Named Zando Central Market, the building replaces a historic market on the same site in Kinshasa that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.

Think Tank Architecture was brought in to design the replacement market after the original building had already been torn down. The studio used this as an opportunity to completely reimagine the role and function of the market, while taking visual cues from the original building and others like it in the city.

Alongside an increased number of vendor stalls, the 82,000-square-metre replacement incorporates storage space, a fire station, a police station, a medical centre, a vet’s, offices and a food court.

“The fresh market is on the same site as the ancient one, on the 3.7-hectare plot,” Think Tank Architecture told Dezeen.

“However, the building’s footprint has been totally redefined, taking into consideration the scale of the program and the urban context,” it continued.

Industry observers note that “We wanted it to be an African market, and not an interpretation of it. Our comprehension comes from academic, historic and architectural research, dialogue with the client and then visits to other markets in Kinshasa.”.

It has been revealed that zando Central Market has a rectangular proposal measuring 245 metres in length and 150 metres in width. It contains 650 shops with space for 20,000 vendors, which is “more than 5 times its original capacity”, according to the studio.

At its heart is the central covered market, spanning two double-height levels, with three large entrances and outward views used to orient visitors.

It is surrounded by a three-storey building containing the other facilities. Landscaped patios punctuate the plan, carving out space for public squares and informal markets to take place.

“It’s an key part of our approach to keep the building open to the public, including the more modest,” said Think Tank Architecture.

Industry observers note that the material palette for the project comprises brick and concrete, chosen to be in keeping with the local context and skills of the region’s construction workers. Demolition waste from the original market was used in the substructure.

“We are quite happy to say that this project reactivated three terracotta factories within a 60-kilometre distance from the market,” reflected the studio.

It uses a mushroom-slab structural system, in which the columns flare at their top, referencing the original market’s design.

Meanwhile, the perforated brick facades were designed to facilitate natural ventilation and provide shade from the sun.

In tandem with the thermal mass from the concrete, this helps cool the building, minimising the need for technical cooling equipment and keeping project costs low.

Interior finishes were also kept deliberately simple for cost reasons. However, the perforations of the facades help add flourish, evoking moucharabiehs – a type of projecting oriel window enclosed with wooden latticework, typically seen in traditional Islamic architecture.

Zando Central Market is on the eight-strong shortlist for the civic project category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Sydney Fish Market by 3XN and TCC DAKA Renewable Resource Recycling Center by KPF.

It is yet to officially open, as the second phase of the project – involving the renovation of the surrounding streets – needs to be completed to allow access.

According to recent reports, “This phase of works is under the city’s supervision and is going slower,” mentioned Think Tank Architecture. “We hope, and it’s in our client’s interest, that the market will be able to open by the end of this year.”.

Other market architecture recently featured on Dezeen includes the multi-level Tepoztlán Market in central Mexico by local studios Ramírez Suarez Arquitectos and Laboratorio Regional de Arquitectura, and an open-air market in Colombia designed by Tarq Studio to accommodate community gatherings.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we first met Marco Baravalle in 2015 at the 56th Venice Biennale, All the World’s Futures, when we were organizing with the Gulf Labor Coalition.
  • Through Baravalle, a longtime researcher, curator, and activist, we encountered a network of autonomous spaces in Venice and Milan.
  • Eleven years later, The Battleground of Art: Radical Curating in the Crisis of Neoliberalism (2026) extends this praxis into an important and timely call to action.

Sources indicate that we first met Marco Baravalle in 2015 at the 56th Venice Biennale, All the World’s Futures, when we were organizing with the Gulf Labor Coalition. The group and our autonomous direct-action wing, Global Ultra Luxury Faction (G.U.L.F.), had been invited by curator Okwui Enwezor to present our research and organizing against migrant worker exploitation in the construction of the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi. An artist boycott was underway, direct actions were escalating, and days earlier, on May 1, we had shut down the Guggenheim Museum in Fresh York City.

Through Baravalle, a longtime researcher, curator, and activist, we encountered a network of autonomous spaces in Venice and Milan. These were not simply cultural centers; they formed the infrastructure for collective organizing, resistance, and enacting other worlds.

Eleven years later, The Battleground of Art: Radical Curating in the Crisis of Neoliberalism (2026) extends this praxis into an important and timely call to action. Drawing on his two decades of experience, Baravalle offers what we have called movement-generated theory and practice, rooted in the dialectic of doing and knowing. The book confronts the neoliberal capture of the art world, while also excavating histories and practices of abolition and autonomy that offer other possibilities.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A former Philadelphia Museum of Art executive admitted on Friday to using company credit cards to make approximately $30,000 in personal purchases, the Inquirer reports.

Latasha Harling, the museum’s former chief people and diversity officer, pleaded guilty to receiving stolen property, averting a trial that had been scheduled for Friday.

Common Pleas Court Judge Leon King II sentenced Harling, 44, to five years of probation for the misdemeanor offense. King also ordered her to pay the museum $30,000 in restitution in monthly installments of at least $500, beginning in January. If she pays the full amount before her probation ends, however, Harling may request early termination of her probation. Related Articles Former Philadelphia Museum CFO Claims Severance Was Withheld as 'Retaliation' Comcast Cofounder Gives $20 M. to Philadelphia Museum of Art, One of its Largest Gifts, To Greatly Expand Education Spaces.

Harling joined the museum in November 2023 as its inaugural chief people officer (CPO), overseeing human resources and diversity initiatives. Her budgetary responsibilities, the Inquirer noted, included access to corporate credit cards. An affidavit of probable cause filed in connection with her arrest recounts how museum officials grew suspicious of her activities in January 2025, after being alerted to a series of significant, seemingly personal purchases on her credit card statements. A subsequent audit by the museum’s chief financial officer found that Harling had charged $58,885 in personal expenses to the card since her hiring.

Harling was offered the opportunity to repay $32,565 to the museum, the affidavit states. She resigned shortly thereafter, with the credit card expenses still outstanding. The museum then sought to recover the money: The following February, Harling signed a promissory note agreeing to repay $19,380 over three months. After receiving no payments by April, the museum contacted police.

A spokesperson for the museum mentioned in a statement that its officials are “grateful that the case” is resolved and that “we look forward to returning our focus to the exhibitions, programs, and experiences we provide for our community.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the University of California, San Diego will open a 12,000-sq.-ft contemporary art space on its campus in spring 2027. Housed in the university’s new Triton Center, the Strauss Family Gallery will include four indoor exhibition spaces and an outdoor sculpture terrace. Free and open to the public, the Strauss will host exhibitions, commissions, artist residencies and public programmes that encourage collaboration between artists and UC San Diego researchers and scholars.

Jessica Berlanga Taylor, UC San Diego’s chief campus curator, tells The Art Newspaper that the university is aware of the challenges other San Diego cultural institutions are facing and believes investing in art and culture is essential. "The Strauss represents a long-term commitment that the university is making to contemporary art and sees it as an integral part of the university's intellectual and public life," she claims.

In a recent development, in 2023, the local philanthropists Matthew and Iris Strauss gave more than 100 works form their art collection to UC San Diego. (Matthew, who made his money in real estate, died the following year.) Represented artists in the gift include Carrie Mae Weems, Fred Wilson, Zhang Huan and Sabine Moritz.

The Strauss’s fresh David and Claire Guggenheim Gallery will serve as the public entrance and a space for exhibitions, gatherings and an artist-in-residence programme focused on digital artists, while the two-story Gray Box will accommodate large-scale sculpture, moving-image installations and performances.

The 3,043-sq.-ft Black Box will be equipped for immersive video, sound, sculpture and performance; and the White Cube will provide a more conventional gallery setting for works from the Strauss Family Foundation, travelling exhibitions and collaborations with collections in San Diego and beyond.

Taylor calls the Strauss the first "ground-up museum" at UC San Diego. Pointing to existing spaces on campus like the Mandeville Art Gallery (open for nearly 60 years) and a black-box theatre in the music department, she indicates the Strauss will strive to be part of the landscape of both the campus and San Diego at large. But the Strauss will play a unique role—with commissions, curatorial research and exhibitions in collaboration with artists from across the globe.

Industry observers note that UC San Diego’s Stuart Collection, which includes sculptures installed across campus, has already established a public art presence at the university. The Strauss will now give artists a dedicated space for exhibitions, commissions and research.

According to recent reports, “We’re connecting art inside with art outside now with the Strauss and the Stuart Collection, but we also want to distinguish very clearly what Stuart is about and what the Strauss will achieve," Taylor says. "The Strauss is very much about perception and experience, but it’s also about expanding our ways of knowing and presenting different forms of knowledge that you wouldn’t necessarily encounter in the classroom.".

It has been revealed that taylor's greater vision is to engage the community through public programming and student involvement. The Strauss prepares to engage both established and emerging artists, particularly in the digital space, and support the development of their work. "We're looking at how we can bring artistic inquiry into university teaching and research," Taylor says.

This could include incorporating exhibitions and artistic methodologies into existing courses, giving students opportunities to participate in curatorial research and creative projects, and developing collaborations across the university. Taylor points to potential partnerships with UC San Diego’s Qualcomm Institute, the Interdisciplinary Computing and the Arts programme, the Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the Goeddel Family Technology Sandbox as examples of the range of possibilities.

"We see the Strauss as more of a platform than a container for a collection," Taylor indicates. "We do have a collection, but our goal is to be a platform for research and critical inquiry—and for challenging assumptions.".

The Gatto trailer is dividing opinion over Pixar's new painterly style

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that the concept art and early teasers revealed a painterly 2D style.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gatto is a huge departure for Pixar. It will be the first time in the Disney-owned studio's 40-year history that it has strayed from the 3D animation style that it popularised through franchises like Toy Story, Monsters Inc and Incredibles.

It has been revealed that the concept art and early teasers revealed a painterly 2D style. Now Pixar's released a complete trailer, providing a deeper look at the newly introduced hybrid animation approach. And it's really got people talking.

If you want to take advantage of Black Friday to upgrade your own studio setup, see our guides to the best laptops for animation and the best drawing tablets.

The Gatto trailer reveals more details about the movie's premise. Nero is a Mark Ruffalo-voiced black cat who joins the mog mob in Venice. After losing eight of his nine lives, he reevaluates his place in the world and decides to make a fresh start with a street musician called Maja, played by Bianca Babaşa.

The trailer also allows us to see Pixar's hybrid animation style in action. As we already knew, this isn't traditional 2D work. Pixar's combining computer-generated animation with hand-painted 2D textures and shaders.

The environments, characters and sets are modeled and animated in 3D to retain spatial depth, dynamic lighting and camera movement. The studio then applies hand-drawn details and a flattened perspective layered onto the 3D models, somewhat like the approach Disney used in its 2012 short Paperman.

Industry observers note that in the comments on YouTube, a lot of people are pleased to see that the movie looks like its concept art (unlike Disney's Hexed). The question is whether Pixar has managed to find the sweet spot at which its familiar 3D models and the stylised 2D art style gel.

For the most part, I think it does. There are moments where the trailer feels a little uncanny, like when the police appear towards the end, and this hybrid style doesn't entirely replicate the warmth of physical animation, but the environments look spectacular, and the flat perspective and visible brushwork give the movie an appealing storybook feel.

Some people were hoping for something even more stylised and feel that Pixar's heart isn't in this approach. There are suggestions that it's chasing a trend on the heels of Into the Spider-Verse and Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem without going all the way there.

Sources indicate that but it might have taken many fans aback if Gatto had made such a radical departure. Sony Pictures Animation could make a movie like Into the Spider-Verse because it wasn't so synonymous with a particular house style. Pixar had to find its own sweet spot.

Industry observers note that people are also seeing the influence of Oscar-winning Flow and DreamWorks' 2022 movie Puss in Boots: The Last Wish. That's fine; there's always room for more cats in animation. Maybe all of these films were inspirations, but the characters and story make Gatto still feel like a Pixar movie even if it looks very different, and that's something that's exciting to see.

Gatto will be released on 5 March 2027.

Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

Print Center Newly introduced York, home to programs and exhibitions celebrating all the art that's pressed, proofed, and published, unveiled Yukiko Yamagata as its new executive director this week.

Her professional profile doesn't immediately scream “print nerd”: Yamagata most recently served as deputy director at Creative Time and previously worked at the Open Society Foundations, where she led a $15.8 million arts and culture fellowship program for socially engaged artists. But one of her earliest roles in the 1990s was as a senior curatorial assistant in the photo department at the Whitney Museum of American Art, and she is a current board member of Women Photograph, an organization focused on equitable practices in photojournalism and visual media.

Yamagata succeeds Judy Hecker, who announced her decision to step down earlier this year after a decade in the role, and is now executive director emerita.

The Women's Studio Workshop in Rosendale, Latest York, dedicated to the printing arts as well as papermaking, bookbinding, photography, and more, has named Natalie Renganeschi as its fourth-ever executive director in the organization's 52-year history.

Renganeschi's career at WSW began in 2018, when she joined as a part-time employee while working as a high school art teacher. Now, she will oversee the nonprofit's major campus expansion, including the relaunch of its ceramics center.

It has been revealed that “My path to leadership hasn’t been a traditional one, but it’s rooted in the ethos of WSW,” Renganeschi said in a statement. “Just as our mediums are steeped in process and the history of craft, working here is a sustained act of communal learning that allows for growth to come from below and within.”.

Gabriel Moses — the photographer behind some of the most influential fashion campaigns in recent years — will receive the Trailblazer Award at The Fashion Awards 2026.

The British Fashion Council (BFC) announced that Gabriel Moses will receive the award at The Fashion Awards ceremony at the Royal Albert Hall in London on November 30.

Previous recipients of the Trailblazer Award include fashion designers Kim Jones, Sarah Burton, and Alessandro Michele — making Moses’ recognition a significant milestone as a photographer and highlighting his growing influence on the fashion industry.

It has been revealed that “Gabriel is one of those rare creative talents whose work has an unmistakable visual language and emotional resonance,” Laura Weir, Chief Executive, British Fashion Council, says in a press release. “Across fashion, music, film and art, he has helped shape contemporary visual culture, while opening up fresh perspectives and inspiring a generation of creatives. We’re delighted to celebrate Gabriel at The Fashion Awards this year and recognise the extraordinary contribution he continues to make to British and global creative culture.”.

A post shared by Gabriel Moses (@gabrielomoses).

According to recent reports, gabriel Moses is a British-Nigerian photographer and filmmaker from South London, known for his distinctive visual style and ability to turn deeply personal stories into striking images that have made an impact across fashion, music and art. Making his directorial debut with Nike at just eighteen years old, Moses established the foundations of a creative practice rooted in storytelling, identity and community. Entirely self-taught, he has since redefined the possibilities of contemporary image-making, making history as the youngest photographer to shoot a Dazed cover at just 22.

Recent findings suggest that his creative portfolio spans campaigns and collaborations with some of the world’s most influential fashion houses and cultural institutions, including Louis Vuitton, Dior, Burberry and Moncler, alongside portraits of cultural figures such as Pharrell Williams, Jay Z, Rihanna, Lauryn Hill, Grace Jones, Cher, Travis Scott, among others. In 2024, Moses released his first monograph Regina.

“It’s a blessing to receive such a prestigious award, I’ve put a lot of heart into my practice from the moment I started and moments like this are a testament to honest work,” Moses says. “I’m grateful to the long list of collaborators who have trusted my ideas.”.

Architecture studios Formafantasma and Gonzalez Haase AAS have worked with Ferrari Style creative director Rocco Iannone on the brand’s first permanent store in New York, clad in a metallic facade.

Located in Manhattan’s SoHo neighbourhood, the flagship store for Ferrari’s fashion label is in a long, narrow building at the corner of Prince Street and Mercer Street and spreads across two levels.

Berlin-based Gonzalez Haase AAS clad the building in brushed metal, with curved window mullions covering floor-to-ceiling glass along its length.

Sources indicate that under Iannone, the team referenced the Ferrari Officina concept, a central theme of the brand that seeks to connect fashion and automotive. It considers “the workshop as a junction at which artistic instinct, scientific rigour, craftsmanship and mechanical precision converge,” according to the team.

“The Officina is the place where intuition is given form through discipline, and where the human touch works in harmony with mechanical precision,” said Iannone.

The opening follows another Ferrari Style store opened earlier this year in London, designed by the same team, and both stores share pops of red, warm beige finishes, and steel accents.

However, the Latest York space was designed to fit in with the city. The team said the New York location reflects the “form, scale and material character of SoHo”.

“For New York, we wanted to translate this spirit into a space in which architecture, fashion and object design each retain their own identity while contributing to a single Ferrari language,” mentioned the team.

“Every material and detail has been chosen to express this balance between art and science, creating an environment that is open, evolving and in direct dialogue with the energy of SoHo.”.

Men’s ready-to-wear is located on the first floor, with objects displayed on units designed by Formafantasma.

The space is bordered by a deep red curtain and large rectangular ceiling lights.

A staircase to the left side of the store leads to the “more intimate” second level, containing women’s ready-to-wear, footwear and accessories collections.

It also contains the store’s atelier, the second worldwide apart from the London location.

It has been revealed that wrapped in leather curtains, the space provides a private setting for personalisations and alterations. A table containing samples of textiles and hardware sits at the centre.

Ferrari Style, the brand’s luxury fashion line founded in 2021, has other US locations in New Jersey, Miami, and Las Vegas.

Ferrari recently unveiled a laptop collaboration with HP, as well as its first electric vehicle earlier this year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that HESSE FLATOW is pleased to announce the opening of Franklin, an exhibition of paintings and works on paper by Nat Meade, marking his third solo presentation with the gallery. The show is on view through April 18, 2026.

According to recent reports, the emotional arc of life’s struggles and triumphs take shape within Meade’s figurative works, reflecting the artist’s everyday experiences as he navigates being a father, son, partner, and academic. Far from portraits of actual individuals, his protagonists mirror timeless archetypes. At times, we encounter a lone traveler searching for existential validation; at other times, we see through intergenerational dynamics. This allegorical distance via painting provides a realm for Meade to explore personal challenges through absurd, somber, and humorous tropes, while also furnishing a space rife with human nature that bears unequivocal resonance.

Sources indicate that meade’s reflections on his relationship with his father after his recent passing, and subsequent reevaluations of his own role as a parent percolate throughout the works in the exhibition. Vulnerability, pain, and mortality are themes Meade does not shy away from, yet the introduction of younger males in this body of work casts a sense of hope, acceptance, reconciliation, and renewal.

Faced with a pair of dangling legs from a cloud in Poise, we question whether a figure is ascending or descending from the heavens, a suggestion perhaps on the interchangeability of birth and death, be it physical or spiritual. Ghostly specters hover over certain individuals – a metaphor for inherited trauma and release. In the same way that a soul peels away from an expiring body in classic cartoons, we observe a spirit looking back on itself with what might be  happiness or regret. The exhibition’s title Franklin is a subtle nod to the 1974 horror film Texas Chainsaw Massacre, known for its portrayal of a deranged patriarchal family. Meade embraces this inner turmoil of contending with one’s violent and antagonistic impulses as his characters are visibly sublimated or put in their place. A vulture picking away at a corpse recalls the eternal punishment of Prometheus by Zeus, while a bearded figure on his hands and knees echoes William Blake’s portrayal of Nebuchadnezzar, condemned for his lust for power.

In contrast to the adults, Meade’s younger figures appear more harmonious. A young boy charts his own path as he steers a boat with a radiant torch, unclouded by societal and familial pressures. A sense of childlike wonder and adventure beholds an adolescent ankle-deep in a secluded cove, reaching in to touch the sea floor brilliantly covered in starfish, anemones, and mussels. In a related work, we observe two pairs of legs belonging to father and son in the same shallow pool, one tenderly guiding the other. Having in the past shown his figures wrestling with or victims of forces of nature, physically being overtaken by turbulent wind and crashing waves, Meade’s focus on calmer seas signals a turning point. He recognizes the need to acknowledge one’s rocky histories in order to heal and release future generations from similar burdens. Despite what may seem like an insurmountable heaviness, he reminds us of the stubborn resilience of human nature, making progress attainable.

Sources indicate that ahead of the Museum of Modern Art's (MoMA) annual benefit for its Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center tonight, November 12, about 20 protesters assembled outside the institution to call on the gala's honoree, Steven Spielberg, to reject the recognition. The protest comes amid growing calls to oust Leon Black from the museum board over his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Playwright and theater artist Gracie Gardner was held by security after she entered the museum and chanted in protest of Leon Black. She was subsequently issued a No Trespass Order banning her from MoMA for life and released by security.

Another letter sent to Spielberg by the feminist campaign group We Are UltraViolet, reviewed by Hyperallergic, urges the Academy Award-winning director to boycott MoMA until the institution severs ties with Black and renames the film venue.

It has been revealed that “MoMA has benefited so handsomely from Black that they have named the very room you will be honored in, the Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center, in his honor,” reads the missive to Spielberg, authored by Elisa Batista, campaign director of UltraViolet. For the past four iterations of the benefit, MoMA has funneled all proceeds into the film center, which was created in 2019 in recognition of a $40 million gift from the private equity tycoon.

According to recent reports, “Mr. Spielberg, you do NOT want your legacy connected to accused abuser and Epstein associate Leon Black,” Batista continues.

The letter makes reference to three sexual assault and misconduct accusations brought forth against the billionaire, all of which Black “more than denies,” according to his representative. One of the lawsuits was discontinued by the plaintiff, and an earlier lawsuit was dismissed by the court. A third lawsuit was initially allowed to move forward after a judge imposed a sanction on the law firm and plaintiff for falsifying evidence, but dismissed with prejudice last month after the plaintiff said she was “medically incapable of continuing,” as reported by the Guardian. “My request [to dismiss the case with prejudice] is not a concession concerning the truth of my allegations, a retraction of my statements, or an acceptance of defendant’s disputed positions; it reflects only the medical reality that I can no longer safely pursue this litigation,” Jane Doe wrote in a legal filing, according to the Guardian.

UltraViolet mentioned it has not received a response from Spielberg's representatives.

It has been revealed that black left his role as CEO of his private equity firm Apollo Global Management in 2021, when news broke that he paid Epstein $158 million for financial advice from 2012 to 2017, after Epstein’s first conviction for soliciting sex from a minor. Even though he stepped down as MoMA board chairman that same year, after Hyperallergic published an open letter signed by over 150 artists calling for his removal, Black remains a MoMA board trustee.

It has been revealed that public scrutiny of Black intensified in September, after the US House of Representatives unanimously approved a resolution to hold the MoMA trustee in contempt of Congress for defying subpoenas in an Epstein investigation. This month, Black sued California Representative Robert Garcia for defamation over public comments such as "Leon Black is at the center of Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.”.

Gardner told Hyperallergic at tonight's protest that she was “amazed” by the public response to the open letter to Spielberg she initially posted on her Instagram in September.

“Steven Spielberg has made his career making stories about the dignity of women and children,” Gardner continued. “It's totally disgusting that he's accepting an award [at the film center named after Leon Black], who's presently in contempt of Congress for not producing NDAs and his involvement in the Epstein files.”.

Last month, Gardner co-performed a staged reading of former Barclays CEO and JP Morgan executive Jes Staley's deposition on Epstein to the United States House Oversight Committee in July.

In a recent development, at this evening's protest, others carried signs pointing to Black's connections to pro-Israel and Zionist organizations. Black has reportedly donated money to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which denies that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, and Birthright Israel, which is accused of serving as a propaganda campaign for the Israeli government.

“I can personally say I'm Jewish and it's specifically because of my Jewish values that we're here. Never again means never again for anyone,” one demonstrator, Janet Goodman-Clarke, told Hyperallergic. “Leon Black not only is a Zionist, but he's also named ad nauseam in the Epstein files.”.

MoMA has not replied to Hyperallergic's request for comment.

Recent findings suggest that artists, activists, and Epstein survivors have repeatedly gathered in front of MoMA demanding his ousting. Among those in attendance at today's action was Katie Fuller, arts educator and founder of the Time and Memory Project, who staged a separate protest calling for Black's removal in front of the museum with her sister in September.

Industry observers note that last month, Fuller teamed up with Epstein survivors, UltraViolet, and the Epstein-Trump Reading Room, created by the Institute for Primary Facts, to illustrate the extent of Epstein's network. The free, mobile installation displayed a timeline of President Donald Trump’s relationship with Epstein and contains thousands of books' worth of the released so-called “Epstein Files,” in which Black was mentioned over 8,500 times.

That protest included Dani Bensky, a dancer, educator, and Epstein survivor from 2004 to 2005. A few weeks after the action, Bensky wrote an op-ed for Hyperallergic condemning Black’s board position as “one of the starkest examples of institutional ignorance — a head-in-the-sand, look-the-other-way mentality that will inevitably give abuse of power a dark corner to grow and fester in.”.

Besides his investments in MoMA, Black has held enormous sway in the art world. In a newly released book by William D. Cohan, Black disclosed plans to convert the Woolworth Mansion into a tax-beneficial art foundation, which is expected to house works from his estimated $5 billion art collection, an asset that Epstein helped leverage as bank collateral.

It has been revealed that gardner noted she had one simple message for the attendees of tonight’s benefit gala: “If you know, you're human garbage. And if you didn't know, you can't say that after tonight, because we're out here saying hi to everybody with our signs.”.

Whitney Museum Is Selling a de Kooning Painting Just Three Years After Receiving It

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fresh York’s Whitney Museum is selling a Willem de Kooning painting at Christie’s next week, just three years after it formally received the work as a gift from the family of one of its former presidents.
  • It has been revealed that yellow River (1958), a large abstract picture dominated by hefty sweeps of blue and yellow, has an estimate of $12 million to $18 million and will appear in Christie’s 20th century evening sale on November 17.
  • Solinger, a lawyer and collector who became the Whitney’s first president from outside the Whitney family in 1966.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh York’s Whitney Museum is selling a Willem de Kooning painting at Christie’s next week, just three years after it formally received the work as a gift from the family of one of its former presidents.

It has been revealed that yellow River (1958), a large abstract picture dominated by hefty sweeps of blue and yellow, has an estimate of $12 million to $18 million and will appear in Christie’s 20th century evening sale on November 17. The painting is being sold to benefit the museum’s collection, according to Artnet News, which first reported the story and the auction house’s catalog. Related Articles Christie's Posts Highest Watch Total Ever and Sells Bulgari Pink Diamond for $14 M. As Art Week NYC Kicks Off, Galleries Have Millions of Dollars of Art to Sell--And No Shortage of Naras.

Yellow River belonged to David M. Solinger, a lawyer and collector who became the Whitney’s first president from outside the Whitney family in 1966. Solinger bought the painting from Sidney Janis Gallery in 1959, and according to Christie’s, he liked it so much that it hung for a time at the foot of his bed, where he could see it every morning.

In a recent development, following Solinger’s death in 1996, the painting passed to his wife, Betty Ann Besch Solinger, who promised it to the Whitney in 2011. The work was exhibited at the museum that year, but the gift was not formally completed until 2023, after she passed in 2022. Now, three years later, it is headed back to the market.

This isn’t the first time the Whitney has dabbled with deaccessioning, the practice of selling works from a museum’s permanent collection. In 2023, the museum sent a group of paintings by Edward Hopper, Maurice Prendergast, John Marin, and others to Sotheby’s. It was led by Edward Hopper’s Cobb’s Barns, South Truro (1930–33), which came with an $8 million to $12 million estimate.

At the time, Jane Panetta, then the Whitney’s curator and director of the collection, told ARTnews that the sales were part of a broader effort to expand and diversify the museum’s holdings.

“We’re always thinking about how one defines ‘the museum of American art,’ being mindful of wanting the collection to accurately represent the United States,” Panetta said. “We think that means the collection has to evolve. We have to try and close critical gaps, and having endowment funds for acquisitions is a key means to doing that.”.

Sources indicate that in fact, the Whitney’s 2023 Collection Strategic Blueprint recommended making deaccessioning a more regular part of the institution’s collecting strategy, particularly in areas where it already holds a substantial amount of work. The museum still has several major paintings by de Kooning, including Door to the River (1960), which dates from roughly the same period as Yellow River.

Painted in 1958, Yellow River belongs to a particularly important moment in de Kooning’s career, when he was moving away from the figures of his celebrated “Woman” paintings toward increasingly abstract compositions inspired in part by the landscape and highways around New York. The painting was included in his 1959 exhibition at Sidney Janis Gallery, where, according to Christie’s, 19 of the 22 works had sold by noon on opening day.

In a recent development, deaccessioning remains a touchy subject in the museum world, though the Association of Art Museum Directors says it’s acceptable for institutions to use proceeds from sales to acquire fresh works or pay for the direct care of their collections. According to the Whitney’s collections policy, works are intended to remain in the collection permanently, while sales that would improve or refine its holdings are generally okay.

Tech Report: Ocean liner sunk in Florida to become "world's largest artificial reef"

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (535 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography courtesy of Destin-Fort Walton Beach.
  • On Wednesday, the ocean liner SS United States was sunk 180 feet underwater to become an artificial reef off the coast of Florida.
  • The sinking took approximately eight hours, and dozens of onlookers and officials looked on as the ship underwent a controlled deployment, or scuttling, to the bottom of the ocean.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of Destin-Fort Walton Beach.

On Wednesday, the ocean liner SS United States was sunk 180 feet underwater to become an artificial reef off the coast of Florida.

The sinking took approximately eight hours, and dozens of onlookers and officials looked on as the ship underwent a controlled deployment, or scuttling, to the bottom of the ocean.

The ship will join a long stretch of artificial reefs, including 580 other decommissioned vessels and structures, that line the ocean floor off the coast Destin-Fort Walton Beach, Florida.

“A new chapter has begun in Destin-Fort Walton Beach, Florida, where the legendary SS United States, once the fastest ocean liner in the world, has completed her final voyage to become the World’s Largest Artificial Reef,” noted a release from the government of Destin-Fort Walton Beach.

The site serves as a tourist and dive destination for SCUBA divers both new and seasoned, as the underwater structures are meant to provide infrastructure for marine life.

“Beyond its appeal as a dive destination, the SS United States will serve an vital environmental purpose,” said the team.

“Her massive structure will provide newly introduced habitat for marine life, supporting the growth of an underwater ecosystem that includes inhabitants such as sea turtles, grouper, snapper and marlin.”.

In preparation for its scuttling, the ship underwent a years-long remediation process, where it was stripped of toxic materials, such as green neotex exterior floor covering and paint.

Elements such as the ventilation system, wiring and the propeller were also removed, with the latter stored for a land-based museum that will accompany the dive site.

“To see a project of this magnitude become a reality is an incredible moment for our team and for the future of marine conservation,” said Destin-Fort Walton Beach natural resources chief Alex Fogg.

“This is so much more than creating a fresh dive destination. It’s an opportunity to advance marine science on a scale we’ve never experienced before. The sheer scale of the SS United States presents a rare opportunity to study how an artificial reef of this size transforms over time.”.

The project has been years in the making. The ship, designed by naval architect William Francis Gibb and known for its speed, served as a passenger vessel between 1952 and 1969.

It was decommissioned in 1969, and eventually bought to a Philadelphia harbour in the 1990s, where it sat inactive for decades as various owners bought and then sold the vessel in failed attempts to restore it and make it profitable.

In 2009, the non-profit SS United States Conservancy purchased and began stewarding the ship.

In 2024, due to rent concerns, the ship could no longer stay berthed at its Philadelphia pier, and the SS United States Conservancy sold it to Okaloosa County, Florida, for $1 million.

As of today, it stands upright in its intended position, and its uppermost deck is accessible to divers, who can “now enjoy the site”.

Other artificial reefs around the world include the Reefline project in Miami, which is set to feature underwater sculpture designed by OMA and a LEGO-inspired modular system designed by Alex Goad, intended to restore damaged coral reefs.

Photography courtesy of Destin-Fort Walton Beach.
