💡 Key Takeaways
  • PPOW are pleased to present Orchid Rain on the Underground, Chris “Daze” Ellis’s third solo exhibition with the gallery.
  • Born in Brooklyn in 1962, Daze became inspired by early graffiti writers like Blade, Lee Quiñones, and PHASE 2 while attending High School of Art and Design in the mid 1970s.
  • According to recent reports, inspired by early 20th-century urban realist artists, including John Sloan of the Ashcan School and Reginald Marsh of the WPA era, Daze’s works honor Latest York City’s streets and subways as important sites of his creative evolution.

PPOW are pleased to present Orchid Rain on the Underground, Chris “Daze” Ellis’s third solo exhibition with the gallery. The show is on view through April 25, 2026. Featuring a upcoming series of paintings, multimedia installation, and a site-specific mural, the exhibition harnesses the passion and spontaneity of the graffiti movement of the 1970s and 80s while demonstrating a thoughtful and meticulous practice honed over the past five decades. While the version of New York City that fostered Daze’s beginnings as a fine artist may feel like a bygone era, the works in this exhibition are evidence of its enduring legacy. By revitalizing that foundational energy for the present moment, Daze affirms the continued relevance of those figures and places, and their profound influence on the creative spirit that persists throughout the city today.

Born in Brooklyn in 1962, Daze became inspired by early graffiti writers like Blade, Lee Quiñones, and PHASE 2 while attending High School of Art and Design in the mid 1970s. As he began to establish his own name as an artist, he was also a frequent visitor to what would become historic landmarks of the city’s nightlife, including the Lit Lounge in the East Village, Danceteria on West 21st Street, and the Mudd Club in Tribeca. These nightclubs, which often doubled as art galleries and performance venues, functioned as generative sites of social and artistic experimentation and part of the driving force behind Daze’s early works. By the early 1980s, he had begun transitioning from tagging subway cars to developing a studio practice that encapsulates the ethos of the city.

According to recent reports, inspired by early 20th-century urban realist artists, including John Sloan of the Ashcan School and Reginald Marsh of the WPA era, Daze’s works honor Latest York City’s streets and subways as important sites of his creative evolution. Simultaneously influenced by the lyrical abstraction of works by Joan Mitchell and Willem De Kooning, Daze combines gestural swaths of acrylic and spray paint with detailed renderings of train car interiors, tunnels, and stations. In Gem Spa In the 80s, 2025, Daze depicts the now iconic newspaper stand and candy store that once operated on the corner of St. Mark’s Place and Second Avenue. Gem Spa was a central destination and meeting place for members of the city’s subcultures and is referenced by literary figures like Jack Kerouac and Allen Ginsberg (who called it a “nerve center” of the city). Important people from Daze’s life can be found throughout the composition, among them critic and curator Carlo McCormick as well as artist Martin Wong, who both emerge amongst the crowd in the painting’s foreground. In other works, technicolor throngs of flowers ascend from heaps of urban rubble, representing optimism amidst inequality and the beauty that can arise out of destruction. Throughout the exhibition, these varied combinations of tropical flora and local flowers from the artist’s home in upstate New York function as poignant memorials to what has been lost and hopeful testaments to the beauty and creativity that can still be found around every corner.

The exhibition will also include a site-specific mural, bringing an aspect of Daze’s practice often relegated to the outdoors into the interior setting of the gallery. Covering the walls of a hallway, the mural gives way to the final room of the gallery, featuring a multimedia installation that transports viewers into a composite scene from the artist’s youth. Combining a light-up dance floor and disco ball, actual subway car seats, and a curated track fusing house, disco, hip-hop, and club music, the installation emphasizes the freedom and creative inspiration that arose from these settings, and their importance to Daze’s personal and artistic development. Combining elements from throughout his career, Orchid Rain on the Underground showcases Daze’s never-ending exploration of daily life in Fresh York City while paying homage to the people and places that comprise its vibrant cultural heartbeat.

#54. Breaking: Speed, Drama, and Unapologetic Grain: The Case for Kodak T-Max P3200

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1137 w)

Breaking: Speed, Drama, and Unapologetic Grain: The Case for Kodak T-Max P3200

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1137 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This Film Friday is featuring our favorite low-light film: Kodak T-Max P3200.
  • There are not many super-high-speed options out there in the film world.
  • Kodak T-Max P3200 (TMZ for short) was originally introduced in 1988 as the third member of Kodak’s T-Max family of films, along with T-Max 100 (TMX) and T-Max 400 (TMY).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This Film Friday is featuring our favorite low-light film: Kodak T-Max P3200. T-Max P3200 is one of the fastest films you can load into your favorite 35mm camera and is perfect for a night out if the flash has to stay home or for just scratching that itch you have for superb contrast and graininess.

There are not many super-high-speed options out there in the film world. Ilford manufactures Delta 3200 (in both 35mm and 120, no less), and Kodak has T-Max P3200. Below that, you drop to ISO 800 in color and all the way to ISO 400 for the next fastest B&W film. Back in the day, we had Fujifilm Neopan 1600, Provia 1600, and Natura 1600, among a few other options, but those are long gone. So, the two 3200 films we have on the market fill an crucial role.

Kodak T-Max P3200 (TMZ for short) was originally introduced in 1988 as the third member of Kodak’s T-Max family of films, along with T-Max 100 (TMX) and T-Max 400 (TMY). The T-Max films are noteworthy for their T-grain structure. Similar to Ilford’s Delta films, T-grain films are designed to produce a smoother grain structure that has less grittiness to it and prints and scans more cleanly. But honestly, you will never think of T-Max P3200 as a fine-grained film—quite the opposite, in fact. But that’s OK, because its grain is one of the features we like best about it.

In a recent development, let’s face it. T-Max P3200 is grainy, but grain is the price you will pay for speed. Our recommendation is to embrace grain, learn to appreciate it, and even love it. Grain is the building block of analog images; it is an integral part of how the photo is made. Once you come around to this, your love of black-and-white films will only grow and grow. And if you are already a fan of film grain, there are few films out there that will please you more than P3200. Buy this film for its grain and consider everything else it has to offer as icing on the cake.

Speaking of which, grain is not the only feature T-Max P3200 has going for it. Its other big strength is its speed. The film is marketed as an ISO 3200 film. If you do any sort of research into this film, you will quickly discover that it is really an ISO 800–1000 film (depending on how you develop it). The “P” in P3200 stands for “push”, as in that is what you are essentially doing with this film when shooting it at 3200.

According to recent reports, our suggestion? Forget all of that. It just causes confusion. Think of P3200 as an ISO 3200 film, because among the many things it does well is expose at ISO 3200. Rate this film at its box speed, go out into the dark, and odds will be good that you come home with decent exposures. This reliability at high speeds has long endeared T-Max P3200 to us. In contrast, while there are things we like about Ilford Delta 3200, we almost never expose it at ISO 3200, generally opting for a slower ISO 1600 or even ISO 1000 rating to help ensure decent exposures. In our experience, Delta 3200 needs to be paired with Ilford developers to really hold onto its speed, whereas P3200 doesn’t seem to be quite as picky. With T-Max P3200, we have no fear of rating it for those higher speeds.

Industry observers note that and speaking of higher speeds, T-Max P3200 can actually go even higher. One of our own staff members set out on a mission to see how high he could take P3200. He got it up to ISO 102,400 before he felt like the process (either the film’s sensitivity or his developing) was breaking down. While his results at those absurdly high speeds are grainy beyond belief and have crunched shadows, they do an excellent job of showing the versatility of this film. Even if ISO 102,400 is not your cup of tea, rest assured that the film will handle ISO 6400 or 12800 pretty dang well.

So, you have grain and speed. The third element we love about P3200 is its contrast. T-Max P3200 has dramatic contrast. It is an atmospheric film. Pair it with dramatic light, and the results will be eye-catching. The shadows and highlights on P3200 tend to go toward the extreme, with the shadows getting crunchy and the highlights slipping into bleached white. In good hands, these qualities make for great images; just be mindful that, if the highlights or shadows are key to you, you should meter the image accordingly.

Industry observers note that if you have stuck around this long, we’ll treat you to a little historical “bet you didn’t know”. If you have ever wondered why Kodak has never manufactured this emulsion in medium format, well… they did. They actually tried to make P3200 in 120 but ran into technical problems they could not fix.

Apparently, the emulsion of P3200 is so sensitive that the slight lip from where the tape connects the film to the backing paper was causing a slight pressure mark in the first frame. Kodak couldn’t eliminate it and figured they couldn’t market the film as an “11 exposure” roll film, so the idea got axed. But still, thinking about shooting P3200 in 120 keeps us awake some nights considering the possibilities.

In a recent development, so, that is our review of T-Max P3200. It is a film we use when we know we need the speed (low light). Or when we have an itch for grain and grit (texture). Or when we are hoping for a bit more contrast in our images (drama). We love T-Max P3200 and were heartbroken when Kodak discontinued it in 2012, and we were likewise elated when it was reintroduced in 2018. T-Max P3200 was given a reprieve from death, and all of us film photographers have benefited from its returning to the market. So make sure you have taken the chance to try a roll of it.

Hit up Blue Moon’s website via the link or visit our Portland, Oregon-based shop to enjoy a Film Friday discount on this wonderful film. Today only!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The third annual ARTnews Awards, an editorial project honoring excellence in art achievements at US arts institutions, has just revealed the winners for its 2026 edition. To help select this year’s winners, ARTnews invited five esteemed US-based curators, along with two ARTnews editors, to review exhibitions that opened between August 2025 and July 2026. Traveling exhibitions were only eligible for their first US stop. Each juror nominated 1–3 exhibitions per category. Over the course of two meetings, the jury chose a group of nominees and a winner in each of six categories. Read more about each juror below.

Dittmer Associate Curator of Modern and Contemporary Art, Art Institute of Chicago.

Recent findings suggest that giampaolo Bianconi is at the moment the Dittmer Associate Curator of Modern and Contemporary Art at the Art Institute of Chicago, where he works across acquisitions, exhibitions, and collection displays. His current exhibitions are “Jill Mulleady: The Passenger” and “Tony Cokes: On Boredom.” Bianconi has organized exhibitions by artists including Marwa Arsanios, Charles Atlas, Louise Bourgeois, Edgar Calel, Renée Green, Iman Issa, Ellsworth Kelly, John Knight, Jill Mulleady, Gladys Nilsson, Lorraine O’Grady, and Nora Turato. His H. C. Westermann survey, “Anchor Clanker,” was on view for one year and accompanied by a catalogue that situated the artist within broader histories of postwar American art. His scholarship engages the political economy of artistic form, technology and circulation, and the histories suppressed in standard avant-garde narratives. He speaks widely about contemporary art and is regularly in public conversation with artists.

Recent findings suggest that jordan Carter joined Dia Art Foundation as curator in 2021. At Dia, he has curated and commissioned exhibitions of work by Jo Baer, stanley brouwn, Tony Cokes, Felix Gonzalez-Torres, Renée Green, Maren Hassinger, Mary Heilmann, Agnes Martin, Cameron Rowland, Lucas Samaras, Keith Sonnier, and Haegue Yang, among others. Carter plays a lead role in the development and display of Dia’s permanent collection and oversees the preservation of and programming around its Utah sites—Robert Smithson’s Spiral Jetty (1970) and Nancy Holt’s Sun Tunnels (1973–76)—as well as the stewardship of Cameron Rowland’s Depreciation (2018).

Carter has also held curatorial positions at the Art Institute of Chicago; Centre Pompidou, Paris; Museum of Modern Art, New York; Studio Museum in Harlem, New York; and Walker Art Center, Minneapolis. He received a BA from Brown University, Providence, Rhode Island, and an MA from the Courtauld Institute of Art, London, where he focused on Fluxus and global conceptual art.

Artistic Director of the Hessel Museum, Center for Curatorial Studies, Bard College (CCS Bard).

Lauren Cornell is the Artistic Director of the Hessel Museum, Center for Curatorial Studies, Bard College (CCS Bard). At the Hessel Museum, she has organized surveys of Sky Hopinka, Daniel Steegmann Mangrané, Martine Syms, Leidy Churchman, and Erika Verzutti, as well as career retrospectives of Dara Birnbaum, Stan Douglas, Ho Tzu Nyen (with Tom Eccles and the Singapore Art Museum), and Nil Yalter (with the Museum Ludwig). From 2005 to 2017, Cornell worked at the New Museum in New York, where she also served as Executive Director of its digital art affiliate Rhizome (2005–12).

Ellen Bruss Chief Curator at the Museum of Contemporary Art Denver.

Miranda Lash is the Ellen Bruss Chief Curator at the Museum of Contemporary Art Denver. Throughout her career, she has worked with museums and arts institutions to expand modern and contemporary art collections, commission new artworks, and develop groundbreaking exhibitions and scholarship that foster experimentation. Her curatorial practice moves across a wide range of media and geographies, with particular attention to the ways that place, regional identity, and layered histories shape contemporary art.

At MCA Denver, Lash’s recent projects include solo exhibitions of latest work by Deborah Jack, Suki Seokyeong Kang, Tomashi Jackson, Clarissa Tossin, Eamon Ore-Giron, and Jason Moran, as well as large-scale group exhibitions including “Colorado Currents” (2026), co-curated with Leilani Lynch, and the touring exhibition “Cowboy” (2023), co-curated with Nora Burnett Abrams. Lash served as co–Artistic Director of “The Future is Present, the Harbinger is Home,” the sixth edition of the international art triennial Prospect New Orleans (2024–25), which she co-curated with Ebony G. Patterson. Since 2019, Lash has served on the board of the Joan Mitchell Foundation and right now serves as co-President alongside Paul Ramirez Jonas. Lash holds a BA with honors in the History of Art and Architecture from Harvard University and an MA from the Williams College Graduate Program in the History of Art.

Curator of Special Projects in Contemporary Art, Los Angeles County Museum of Art.

Diana Nawi joined LACMA as Curator of Special Projects in Contemporary Art in 2024. Prior to that Nawi co-curated “Made in L.A. 2023: Acts of Living” at the Hammer Museum with Pablo José Ramirez, and alongside Naima J. Keith, she was the Susan Brennan Co-Artistic Director of “Prospect.5: Yesterday we remarked tomorrow,” a citywide triennial in Fresh Orleans. Working as an independent curator, Nawi has organized exhibitions at the Olivia Foundation, Mexico City; California African American Museum, Los Angeles; Long Museum, Shanghai; and REDCAT, Los Angeles; among others. Prior to her independent work, Nawi held curatorial positions at the Pérez Art Museum Miami and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, Abu Dhabi Project.

Maximilíano Durón is a queer, Chicanx journalist and critic covering contemporary art. His writing focuses on the work of artists of color, specifically Latinx/Chicanx artists, queer artists, and their intersections, as well as curators, collectors, and scholars whose work has transformed the art world. He has been at ARTnews since 2014 and is right now senior editor, managing the publication’s art fair and Top 200 Collectors coverage. Durón is a winner of the 2023 Rabkin Prize for visual art journalists and a founding member of Critical Minded, an initiative that looks to support the work of a diverse intergenerational group of cultural critics of color. He received his undergraduate degree from NYU in journalism and art history.

Alex Greenberger is deputy editor at ARTnews, having started there as an editorial assistant in 2015. He has covered topics ranging from protests against a former Whitney Museum vice chair in 2018 and 2019 to the controversy involving charges of anti-Semitism and harassment in Documenta 15 in 2022. In his criticism, Greenberger has addressed body horror, the history of video art, the legacy of Pablo Picasso, and the work of artists Wangechi Mutu, Wolfgang Tillmans, Marlene Dumas, and innumerable others. His articles have also appeared in Artspace and the Village Voice, and in gallery catalogs. He graduated from New York University with a BA in art history and cinema studies.

Latest Update: Branding: Philadelphia Museum of Art Brand Identity by Gretel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gretel rebuilt the Philadelphia Museum of Art brand identity around a revived griffin, custom Fairmount Serif and Philly street type.
  • According to recent reports, the badge does the heavy lifting.
  • The type tells the same story in two voices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gretel rebuilt the Philadelphia Museum of Art brand identity around a revived griffin, custom Fairmount Serif and Philly street type.

According to recent reports, the badge does the heavy lifting. A black roundel holds a white griffin, redrawn from the museum's 1938 original, with the institution's name set around it in sturdy capitals. The griffin is no invention: several of them sit on the museum's cornices, and merch carrying the old Griffy was already among the museum's best sellers. Gretel unveiled the identity on October 8, 2025, when the museum reintroduced itself under a shortened name; in February 2026 the museum restored its full name and kept the griffin. The brief was to come down the steps and throw the doors wide open, and the work answers with two registers at once: a quiet, refined institution and loud, vernacular programming.

The type tells the same story in two voices. Fairmount Serif is the museum's latest custom institutional face, drawn with Ryan Bugden. It merges the museum's origins as the Pennsylvania Museum and School of Industrial Arts with Philadelphia's working-class heritage, taking serif details from the original seal and the engraved lettering on the museum walls. The research led Gretel to Hess Neobold, a twentieth-century American face cut by Sol Hess, a Philadelphia-born designer who studied at the museum's own school and later succeeded Frederic Goudy at Lanston Monotype.

Alongside it sits a vernacular library, a curated suite of typefaces borrowed from the city's storefronts, restaurants, murals and street vendors. The library is built to grow, with new custom faces commissioned for flagship exhibitions, so the loud register of the brand keeps changing while Fairmount Serif holds the center.

It has been revealed that the system runs across every surface the museum owns. Wayfinding sets giant floor numerals in the stairwell and plain directional signs against the stone walls, while the parking cube carries the roundel over a single WELCOME. Tickets, wristbands, maps and membership cards repeat the same moves at hand scale: big type, small badge, one color at a time. Enamel pins turn the griffin into a keepsake in black, white and pink.

The same logic scales up to the Great Stair Hall, where banners read Linger Longer, Come One Come All and This Is Your Museum, and out to exhibition books and rack cards that let each show pick its own vernacular voice. A digital overhaul with Gone Fishing and Self Aware rebuilt the web experience the same way. Photography by CoCo Hubbeling and Rob Cusick keeps the work grounded in the building.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AltaMed Health Services, a major healthcare provider in Southern California, is opening an art gallery, library and cultural centre to house its art collection in the Los Angeles suburb of Montebello. AltaMed’s collection, more than 50 years in the making, includes works by Laura Aguilar, Graciela Iturbide, Gabriel Orozco and others. Its new 30,000-sq.-ft space, The Alta, opens to the public on Sunday (15 November).

AltaMed began collecting art in the 1970s, based on a belief that art is an integral part of holistic well-being. Since then, its collection has grown to some 4,000 pieces, with about 1,400 of them right now placed in its offices and clinics.

According to recent reports, “Our collection focuses on Chicano art," Cástulo de la Rocha, the president and chief executive of AltaMed (and founder of the collection), noted in a statement. "Because AltaMed was founded as part of the Chicano Movement in the 1970s, because I was active in the Chicano Movement, and because our patients and employees can connect culturally with the art.”.

In recent years, AltaMed has been converting a warehouse on the edge of a shopping mall in Montebello to house its collection. The space will have regular hours for visitors to tour its gallery, see works on shelves and sliding racks in open storage, and watch behind-the-scenes processes of digitisation and conservation. There is also studio space for artist residencies on site.

Patssi Valdez and rafa esparza’s Sacred and Profane Beauty (2026) Courtesy AltaMed.

“The collection is here to serve the communities that AltaMed is focused on in Los Angeles and Orange County, primarily Latino communities,” Pilar Tompkins Rivas, AltaMed’s chief curator and vice president of arts, tells The Art Newspaper. “So we think about art that is relevant and celebratory of those populations.”.

Some recently acquired and commissioned works also address health and community—such as Sonia Romero’s mural The Fence-Pomona (2026), made expressly for the central communal space in a senior-care facility in nearby Pomona. The mural is 6ft high and 10ft wide, depicting a white lattice fence festooned with roses and the San Gabriel Mountains behind it. It ioverlooks a space used for meals, artmaking and gathering for patients.

AltaMed’s collection runs the gamut of media and spans more than 100 years, although most of the work was made after the Second World War. Early pieces include those of Hernando Gonzallo Villa, a commercial artist who famously designed ads and posters for the Santa Fe Railway. More recent works include drawings, prints and paintings by Carlos Almaraz, Judy Baca, Camille Rose Garcia, Gronk, Frank Romero, Eloy Torrez, John Valadez and Linda Vallejo.

The artist Felicia Montes at La Botánica del Barrio (2026) Courtesy AltaMed.

According to recent reports, the first exhibition in the gallery is Patssi Valdez: LA LA LA (until 9 April 2027), featuring photo-based and collage works by a pioneer of Los Angeles’s Chicano art movement. For this show, Valdez re-created some of her photography from the 1970s and 80s—portraits of friends that helped define punk and goth glamour.

She says she had discussed doing something “out of the box” with AltaMed, and several of the framed work have coloured strips of paper flying out from the frame. To highlight some of her portraits, Valdez added Swarovski crystals to the prints, such as in Divine Dede (2026) and Hot Pink (Mario, Charlie & DeDe) (1983/2025). She also co-created work in collaboration with two younger artists, rafa esparza and Gabriela Ruiz.

Sources indicate that it has been more than a decade since Valdez had a solo exhibition. “AltaMed has been a collector of my work for quite a while and has been very supportive," she claims. The organization has purchased Valdez’s paintings and photography, and even one of her signature full-size paper dresses. One of these dresses is in a glass case in The Alta’s open-storage area.

Down the hall are the residency studios. The artist Rubén Esparza is working in one of them, where he has been making multimedia pieces featuring his "ongoing exploration of the cultural significance of Latinx, Chicano and Queer diasporas".

In a recent development, the other studio has been transformed into an educational apothecary by Felicia Montes and her collective Mujeres de Maíz. La Botánica del Barrio (2026) features displays of samplable traditional herbal teas and tinctures, as well as a decorated pushcart. In the hallway, The Wellness Wall lets visitors put up cards with their own home remedies and healing practices. Visitors have suggested some very practical cures—from "talk to friends" and "travelling" to "Vicks" and "a good mezcal".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the documentary series Craft in America returns with two new episodes, streaming online now and premiering on PBS this December. These episodes are part of the Handwork: Celebrating American Craft 2026 initiative, a yearlong project marking the nation’s 250th anniversary and celebrating the diversity of the crafts that define America.

SOUTH and NORTH complete the series’ journey through craft across the United States, which began in December 2025 with episodes EAST and WEST.

The SOUTH episode explores craft artists who are building an inclusive and hopeful future, such as Jessica Osceola, an artist and member of the Seminole tribe of Florida.

Industry observers note that “Making objects is something that we’re just born into,” says Osceola.“Craft links the generations. You’re looking at your past, your present, and your future, and it’s good that the chain never gets broken.”.

Along with Jessica and the Osceola-Zepeda family of Naples, Florida, the episode features Ato Ribeiro, an artist in Atlanta, Georgia, who makes wooden quilts inspired by Ghanaian symbols; fiber artist Vicki Essig, who works with silkworms to create art garments in Spruce Pine, North Carolina; stained-glass mosaic artist Sebastian Duncan-Portuondo in Miami Beach, Florida; and Shaka Zulu and Edward Buckner, who participate in the Black Masking Indian society traditions of New Orleans, Louisiana, known for their elaborate beaded costumes.

Industry observers note that in NORTH, Craft in America investigates the impact of the northern landscape on artists. Jeremy Frey, a featured artist in NORTH, reflects how his work and the environment are deeply connected.

According to recent reports, “There is an invasive insect that’s killing all the trees, the emerald ash borer beetle,” states Frey, a contemporary basketmaker in Eddington, Maine. “We’re losing the material that the baskets are made of … Someday, I might be one of the last people weaving in black ash.”.

The episode also features the annual Intertribal Canoe Journey in the Pacific Northwest; Haystack Mountain School of Crafts on Deer Isle, Maine; artist Sayaka Ganz, who works with reclaimed plastics in Fort Wayne, Indiana; and Tia Keobounpheng in Minneapolis, Minnesota, exploring her Sami ancestry through wood and fiber wall sculptures.

Both episodes are streaming now on the PBS app, pbs.org, and craftinamerica.org.

NORTH and SOUTH premiere on PBS on Friday, December 18, 2026, at 9pm and 10pm (check your local listings), as well as on YouTube.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • I hold no ill will towards this latest generation of fans who I doubt can list every F1 World Champion going all the way back to the 1980s as I can.
  • According to recent reports, after news broke about the latest camera, I simply had to try it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that formula One has changed a lot since I’ve been watching. People used to look at me strangely when I said I enjoyed watching race cars drive around in circles on a Sunday. Now, the sport is swamped by newly introduced fans drawn to the sport via Netflix’s Drive to Survive and Charles Leclerc’s boyish good looks.

I hold no ill will towards this latest generation of fans who I doubt can list every F1 World Champion going all the way back to the 1980s as I can. In fact, without them, I dare say I would never have received the limited edition Leica Q3 43 F1 edition in a brown cardboard box this week.

According to recent reports, after news broke about the latest camera, I simply had to try it. Photography and F1 have a history: Canon sponsored Williams in the team’s glory days; possibly my favourite F1 photo of all time is Nigel Mansell and Ayrton Senna glancing over at each other while driving almost 200 miles per hour in Barcelona in 1991. Their wheels are inches apart from each other, both daring each other to see who will brake first. The sponsor on Mansell’s wing reads ‘Canon.’.

So far as I know, this is Leica’s first-ever foray into F1. The special version of the Q3 43 comes with carbon fiber grips, a material that’s both light and strong, which is why F1 teams have been using it to build cars for the past 40 years.

According to recent reports, the camera comes covered in non-slip microvelour that’s modeled on a racing steering wheel. The pictures really don’t do this material justice; it’s a beautiful touch and I couldn’t stop running my fingers over it, like when you’ve just shaved your head.

In a recent development, that’s not all the F1-inspired hardware, either. The shutter is a soft-release button with a carbon inlay and red rim. It reminds me of an old-school stopwatch, the kind you’d see in a movie about a promising young rookie arriving for testing with an established team at a rain-soaked racetrack somewhere in England. He completes his first lap, the timekeeper clicks the stopwatch, glances at the time, turns to the engineers, and gives a knowing smile. You just know he’s going to be something special.

Having never shot a Leica Q3 of any focal length, I immediately fell in love with it. I mean, it’s just so damn beautiful. It’s a perfectly proportioned camera, and a joy to use. It took me no time at all to set up, and I particularly enjoyed the little ‘zoom’ button that crops into the sensor from the 60-megapixel 43mm to the five-megapixel 150mm end.

And it’s certainly a head-turner. I highlighted it to as many people as I could over the past four days, and everyone was taken with it. The BMXers were particularly impressed with the microvelour finish. My mom called it “handsome.”.

I wanted to shoot some pulsating auto action with it, but I swiftly realized that — despite the F1 logo on the front — it’s not exactly a camera for shooting high-speed objects. It’s still a Leica Q3; it’s a camera that wants you to slow down and think carefully about what you’re shooting. In his review of the Q3 43, Chris Niccolls remarked, “There is a simplicity and a meditative experience to be had, wandering the streets with a compact camera on your shoulder.” That is true.

In a recent development, as I write this, the camera is already on its way back to Leica. I will miss it. But at almost $10,000, it’s very unlikely I will be buying one.

Several museums are joining forces to celebrate Wolf Kahn, who rendered his pastoral surroundings in saturated hues and diffused light, on the occasion of the late artist's 100th birthday next October. Unfolding across 2027, Kahn's centennial program is assembled by the artist's namesake foundation, which recently opened a permanent location for its archives in New York City this summer.

Sources indicate that known for melding the representational with the abstract, Kahn's reputed, lesser-known, and never-before-seen work will be exhibited in locations that shaped his life and career trajectory. Born in 1927 in Germany to a Jewish family, Kahn moved to the United States in 1940 as a refugee during World War II. He got his bearings in New York City, which became an influential home base for the artist throughout his lifetime.

He also spent a significant amount of time developing his practice in Martha's Vineyard and Provincetown, Massachusetts, where he worked as a studio assistant for Abstract Expressionist Hans Hofmann. He eventually purchased a farm in West Brattleboro, Vermont, where he would spend his summers painting en plein air from 1968 until he died in 2020. Over seven decades, Kahn carved out a reputation for rendering nature through luminous, exaggerated, and arbitrary color, creating a glowing effect across his landscapes.

Vaginal Davisfor “Vaginal Davis: Magnificent Product” at MoMA PS1, Latest York (October 9, 2025–March 2, 2026, US debut, following versions at Moderna Museet, Stockholm, and Gropius Bau, Berlin).

According to recent reports, often described as an icon of Los Angeles’s queer and punk scenes, Vaginal Davis has made art that often wasn’t meant for display in museums or galleries. At the core of her practice, spanning performances, zines, videos, installations, and more, is her artistic persona, which imbues her art with ribald, tongue-in-cheek humor, even as she discusses serious topics like race and identity, gender and queerness. Often, her art is designed to shock viewers and make them squirm. In doing so, Davis asks why her pieces would make anyone uncomfortable. “I have never cared for entertaining anyone. My performances may have elements that some may find entertaining, but that’s not my main purpose,” she once told Interview magazine. Related Articles ARTnews Awards 2026 Best Thematic Museum Exhibition: "MONUMENTS" ARTnews Awards 2026 Historical Artist of the Year: Theresa Hak Kyung Cha.

In its US debut at MoMA PS1, “Magnificent Product” presented Davis’s uncanny world, from her days as the front woman for her band ¡Cholita! The Female Menudo during the late ’80s and early ’90s to her time making zines meant for queer people of color, who rarely featured in mainstream magazines. Each of the exhibition’s galleries was highly stylized. Her ephemera archive was installed on walls painted mint green and was obscured by a transparent scrim that was meant to be pushed away by viewers seeking a closer look. For an installation titled The Wicked Pavilion: Tween Bedroom (2021), a bright pink tween bedroom contained a massive plaster phallus on a rotating bed. Screened in a space meant to resemble the now-defunct Cinerama Dome on Sunset Boulevard, her visual album, The White to Be Angry (1999), looks at the insidious nature of white supremacy in the US. As she once put it, it is a “nutters pastiche stabbing toxic masculinity, race, and gender, in the style of an MTV music video, while thrashing thorny filmmakers Clive Barker, Woody Allen, and Bruce LaBruce. Not for the faint of fart.”.

A simple logo redesign has become Australia's latest culture war – why that's bad news for designers

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you'd asked me last month to name the most politically explosive branding project in Australia, I wouldn't have guessed it'd be a local council's email signature.
  • Sutherland Shire Council, in Sydney's south, covers a population of around 240,000 people.
  • Yet in recent weeks, it's been at the centre of a row over its crest: an engraved portrait of Captain James Cook, who first came ashore on Australia's east coast at Kurnell, within the shire, in 1770.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you'd asked me last month to name the most politically explosive branding project in Australia, I wouldn't have guessed it'd be a local council's email signature. But here we are.

Sutherland Shire Council, in Sydney's south, covers a population of around 240,000 people. It rarely gets much coverage in the national press, let alone grabs attention in England over 10,000 miles away.

Yet in recent weeks, it's been at the centre of a row over its crest: an engraved portrait of Captain James Cook, who first came ashore on Australia's east coast at Kurnell, within the shire, in 1770.

According to recent reports, back in July, staff began favouring a newer, simpler logo across its communications. It's a light blue wave that's simple but effectively represents an area on Australia's east coast.

According to recent reports, to be clear, Cook has not been "cancelled", removed or erased by the council. They've simply moved the emblem featuring him to what they call "civic, ceremonial and high-value corporate applications", while using the newer one for things like email signatures, where a simpler mark works better.

Councillor Haris Strangas, though, wasn't happy that he'd never been asked about this change. So he tabled a motion to review the council's policy, then went on the Today show, a major national breakfast TV programme in Australia, to discuss what he'd done.

Admittedly, in the clip, Haris came across as a likeable, ordinary guy who noted he didn't want to inflame the issue and acknowledged most people have better things to talk about. Nonetheless, he wasn't backing down, and as a result, Sutherland Shire found itself a front in Australia's long-running culture wars. Lots of other people then piled in with their own agendas, and you can imagine how it's all spiralled out of control since.

While I imagine most people in the area simply shook their heads and ignored this episode, I think it says something about how politics is making it harder for designers to do their jobs.

In a recent development, logos are tools, not monuments. They need to be tweaked, updated, redesigned or replaced when they start to look tired, or for practical reasons, like when they don't work on small screens. It's not vandalism; it's maintenance.

Ninety-nine per cent of the time, this happens, and nobody bats an eyelid when logo redesigns get it right. Mastercard dropped its name from its circles emblem in 2019. Volkswagen flattened its badge the same year. Burger King reverted to its retro bun in 2021. Pepsi brought back a bolder, blacker globe in 2023. Few people outside the Creative Bloq audience would ever have noticed.

Even changes to the Sunderland Shire logo followed the same pattern. In 2008 the council shrank Cook in favour of its name and a latest colour scheme. Ahead of the 250th anniversary of Cook's landing, it restyled the portrait for digital screens. The wave itself was introduced back in 2017. None of this made the national news.

So what's changed? Well, sadly, we're in an era when a rebrand isn't just a rebrand. If people can make it a symbol of something bigger, they will. It's no longer about colours, type or kerning. It's about identity.

According to recent reports, none of this means history doesn't matter, or that communities shouldn't have a say in how they're represented. But let's be clear: Cook has not been, and has not been, erased. The council just introduced a different design for specific use cases. That's all.

It has been revealed that the fuss that people make over such minor tweaks puts designers in a difficult position. The lesson many clients will take from this, Cracker Barrel, Jaguar et al is that it's safer never to change anything at all. That's bad for design, and frankly bad for the organisations themselves, which end up stuck with identities that no longer work.

It has been revealed that tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

#39. How Understanding Animal Behavior Transforms Your Wildlife Photography

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2602 w)

How Understanding Animal Behavior Transforms Your Wildlife Photography

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2602 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wildlife photography is about more than finding an animal and capturing a sharp image.
  • Most of all, taking the time before you even pick up your camera to learn how to read body language and recognize behavioral patterns can make the difference between reacting to an action and being ready when it happens.
  • It has been revealed that A photograph can show an animal in beautiful detail, but behavior gives the image another layer of meaning and wow factor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wildlife photography is about more than finding an animal and capturing a sharp image. Understanding animal behavior helps photographers anticipate movement, recognize meaningful interactions, and capture moments that reveal more about a subject than its appearance alone—they tell a story.

Most of all, taking the time before you even pick up your camera to learn how to read body language and recognize behavioral patterns can make the difference between reacting to an action and being ready when it happens.

It has been revealed that A photograph can show an animal in beautiful detail, but behavior gives the image another layer of meaning and wow factor. The way an animal moves, feeds, communicates, interacts with others, or responds to its surroundings offers insight into its daily life. Capturing these moments helps tell a more complete story and gives viewers a better sense of the animal beyond its physical appearance.

Industry observers note that behavior also creates opportunities for more compelling compositions. An animal looking directly toward the camera can make an effective portrait, but a photograph of it displaying, feeding, preening, or interacting with another animal can communicate much more. These moments introduce action and context, giving the viewer something to interpret rather than simply observe.

It has been revealed that understanding behavior is particularly valuable because some of the most powerful wildlife photography sits at the intersection of storytelling and documentation of animals’ lives. Animals follow routines and respond to their surroundings according to instinct, environmental conditions, and social relationships. Photographers who recognize these patterns have a better chance of anticipating what might happen next and preparing to capture it.

One of the best ways to become a more effective wildlife photographer is to spend time learning about the animals you want to photograph before heading into the field. Wildlife documentaries, online videos, books, scientific articles, and species-specific resources can all provide useful information about feeding habits, courtship, territorial displays, migration, nesting, and other behaviors. Watching footage can be especially helpful because it allows photographers to see how an animal moves and how one action often leads to another.

However, learning does not have to happen entirely through research. Spending time observing animals in person is just as important, particularly when you can return to the same location regularly. Birds are a common and effective starting point because they are found in a wide range of environments and display an extensive variety of behaviors. Even a local park can offer opportunities to learn how different species feed, interact, defend territory, and respond to people or other animals. To keep things simple, I will focus primarily on birds throughout this article, as their visibility and varied habits make them ideal subjects for study.

When first learning about wildlife photography and animal behavior, simply sitting on a park bench with a book while casually observing nearby birds can be a useful exercise. Watch how they move through their environment, how often they pause to look around, and what they do before taking flight. Notice how their behavior changes when another bird approaches or when people move nearby. With repeated observation, familiar actions become easier to recognize, and you begin to notice patterns that might otherwise go overlooked.

Sources indicate that locations where large numbers of birds gather can be particularly valuable places to practice. For me, rookeries along the New Jersey shore provide opportunities to observe nesting activity, courtship, feeding, and interactions among birds. During winter, the gathering of bald eagles around Conowingo Dam in Maryland offers a chance to watch feeding behavior, competition, and interactions around fish. Areas of open water that attract wintering ducks and geese, including snow geese, are also useful observation sites. When many birds gather in one location, photographers can watch different behaviors happening simultaneously and compare how individual species respond to one another.

To find wildlife hotspots near you, research is key. Look up local Audubon chapters, birding groups, and guided trips—whether on social media or through organized photo walks at nature centers. These communities can be a great source of camaraderie, education, and field assistance.

In a recent development, the goal at these hotspots should be to observe just as much as to photograph. Rather than immediately concentrating on getting a particular image, spend time watching the birds and learning what is happening around you. Notice where they tend to gather, when activity increases, and how they respond to changes in their surroundings. Most of all, returning to the same location can reveal patterns that are difficult to recognize during a single visit.

Sources indicate that animals communicate through more than vocalizations. Posture, movement, positioning, and subtle changes in appearance can all provide clues about what an animal is doing or how it is responding to something nearby. Learning to recognize these signals helps photographers distinguish ordinary activity from moments that may lead to an interesting interaction or display.

Birds provide many visible examples. Changes in posture, feather position, head movements, and wing displays can indicate courtship, aggression, alertness, or preparation for flight. A bird that repeatedly looks in one direction may be responding to another animal or monitoring a potential threat. A change in stance or a sudden pause can also signal that its attention has shifted.

Recent findings suggest that recognizing these signals also gives photographers time to prepare their camera settings. If a bird begins shifting its weight, lowering its body, or opening its wings before taking flight, it may be time to increase the shutter speed and switch to a continuous autofocus mode if you are not already using one. If two birds begin displaying toward each other, consider widening the composition and checking that your shutter speed is fast enough to freeze sudden movement. Small adjustments made before the action begins can make a significant difference.

Recent findings suggest that hunting herons and egrets are great subjects to practice on, as they methodically scour shallow water to snatch up prey. This predictable, repetitive behavior gives you time to observe, learn, and test your own “hunting” skills.

Once photographers become familiar with an animal’s routines, they can begin anticipating what it may do next. Many wildlife behaviors follow recognizable sequences, even though the exact timing can vary. An animal may pause before moving, shift its posture before taking flight, or display a series of movements before interacting with another individual. Recognizing these patterns creates opportunities to prepare for the photograph rather than simply reacting after the action begins.

Sources indicate that camera settings should reflect the behavior you expect to photograph. For a stationary bird or mammal, a shutter speed around 1/500 second is often a useful starting point, although the appropriate speed depends on the focal length, subject movement, and camera stability. For walking animals or birds that are moving more swiftly, 1/1000 second can provide a better chance of freezing motion. Takeoff, flight, running, and fast interactions may require 1/2000 second or faster, particularly when you want to preserve detail in wings or other rapidly moving parts.

Industry observers note that for example, when photographing eagles gathering around a feeding area, a bird preening on a branch may be relatively easy to capture at 1/1000 second. However, if you are anticipating a takeoff or an interaction over a fish, increasing the shutter speed to 1/2000 or 1/3200 second can help freeze the action. Birds in flight against a relatively clear background may also be easier to track with continuous autofocus and subject recognition enabled, depending on the camera system.

It has been revealed that aperture is another notable consideration. When photographing a single animal, a wide aperture such as f/4 or f/5.6 can help separate the subject from a distracting background while allowing more light to reach the sensor. However, when photographing two animals interacting, a slightly narrower aperture may provide enough depth of field to keep both subjects sharp, particularly if they are not positioned on the same focal plane. The trade-off is that a smaller aperture may require a higher ISO or slower shutter speed.

Auto ISO can be useful when photographing unpredictable behavior. Setting a minimum shutter speed and allowing the camera to adjust ISO as light changes can help maintain the speed needed to freeze movement. In rapidly changing conditions, this can be more practical than trying to adjust exposure manually while following an animal. It is still worth keeping an eye on the ISO, especially in low light, to avoid introducing more noise than necessary.

According to recent reports, another useful option is to configure a custom camera button or shooting mode for unexpected action. I set up what I call an “oh heck” setting, which switches my camera to its widest available aperture, a shutter speed of 1/2000 second, continuous autofocus, and burst shooting. When an animal suddenly takes off, starts fighting, or begins an interaction, I can press one button and have the camera ready for action without having to change several settings while the moment is unfolding. Many cameras offer customizable buttons or saved shooting modes that can be configured in a similar way. The exact settings can be adjusted to suit your camera, the subjects you photograph, and the conditions you typically work in, but having a ready-to-go action setup can make a real difference when something happens without warning.

Industry observers note that autofocus settings should also reflect the situation. Continuous autofocus, often called AF-C or AI Servo depending on the camera manufacturer, is generally the better choice when an animal is moving or likely to move. Animal subject detection can help maintain focus as the subject changes position, while a suitable tracking area gives the camera enough flexibility to follow its movement. For a stationary animal, a smaller focus area may offer more precise control, especially when branches, reeds, or other foreground elements could interfere with subject detection.

In a recent development, composition needs to account for movement as well. If you expect an animal to take off, leave room in front of it rather than placing it tightly against the edge of the frame. When photographing feeding or social interactions, a slightly wider composition can preserve the surrounding context and keep crucial parts of the action from being cropped out. You can always refine the composition later, provided the original file retains enough resolution.

It has been revealed that anticipation also requires flexibility. Wildlife does not always follow predictable patterns, and an animal may change direction or abandon an activity without warning. Avoid becoming so committed to one expected moment that you miss something else happening nearby. Keep observing the entire scene, even when you are focused on a particular subject.

Sources indicate that some of the most engaging wildlife photographs involve more than one animal. Social interactions can reveal communication, cooperation, competition, courtship, and relationships between parents and young. These moments often provide a stronger sense of the animals’ lives than an isolated portrait because the photograph captures a relationship or exchange.

Recent findings suggest that photographing interactions requires paying attention to more than one subject. Watch how animals position themselves in relation to each other, how they respond to movement, and whether an encounter is developing into a larger display. The most meaningful part of an interaction may happen swiftly, so it helps to anticipate the sequence rather than concentrate exclusively on a single frame.

Camera settings can become more challenging when multiple animals are involved. If two birds are interacting at close range, a shutter speed of 1/1600 to 1/2500 second can help freeze sudden movements, while an aperture around f/5.6 or f/8 may provide more depth of field than shooting wide open. The exact combination depends on the available light and how far apart the subjects are. If one animal is closer to the camera than the other, even f/8 may not provide enough depth of field to keep both sharp, so consider your shooting angle and focus placement as well.

Autofocus can also be less predictable when animals overlap or move across one another. A camera may switch focus between subjects, particularly when they are close together. If subject detection struggles, adjusting the autofocus area or using a more controlled tracking zone can help. Keeping a little extra room around the interaction also gives you flexibility if the animals move unexpectedly.

It is worth watching what happens after an apparent interaction ends. Animals may continue communicating, move together, or return to a familiar routine. Staying attentive beyond the most obvious action can lead to photographs that reveal more about the relationship between the subjects.

According to recent reports, knowing what is typical for a species helps photographers recognize when something worth capturing is about to happen. Familiarity with everyday routines makes changes in activity easier to notice, whether that means an interaction, a shift to feeding behavior, or a response to changing environmental conditions. Learning about the species and observing it over time provides a more reliable basis for understanding what is happening.

According to recent reports, one example that I often use in my work is that ducks preening in the water often dunk their heads, shake, and then flap their wings to dry off. Knowing this sequence allows me to capture a signature “angel wing” pose time and time again across various species.

Industry observers note that developing an understanding of wildlife behavior takes time. A single outing may provide a few useful observations, but returning to the same locations allows photographers to build a more complete picture of an animal’s routines. Seasonal changes can also influence behavior, making familiar locations worth revisiting throughout the year.

Repeated observation helps photographers become more selective. Instead of photographing every movement, they begin to recognize which moments are likely to produce meaningful images. They may also become more familiar with the best times and locations for observing particular activities, making future outings more productive.

For example, while photographing screech owls, I have often found them resting in tree cavities during the day, but the real action and behavior of these nocturnal predators are best photographed at dusk.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra).

Patience is an important part of this process. Not every visit will result in a memorable photograph, and some of the most useful outings may involve spending more time watching than shooting. That time is still valuable. It builds familiarity with the animals and makes it easier to recognize opportunities when they arise.

Above all, respect for wildlife should remain central to every outing. Maintain appropriate distances, follow local guidelines, and avoid disturbing animals around nesting, feeding, or resting areas. The objective is to document natural behavior, not change it.

Understanding wildlife behavior changes the way photographers approach their subjects. Instead of concentrating only on finding an animal and achieving a technically successful exposure, they begin paying attention to routines, body language, and the relationships between individuals and their surroundings.

The knowledge gained through research and repeated observation makes it easier to anticipate meaningful moments and prepare for them. Whether watching birds at a neighborhood park or spending time at a seasonal gathering, photographers can develop these skills without traveling far from home.

Industry observers note that the strongest wildlife photographs go beyond showing what an animal looks like — they capture a glimpse of how it lives. By learning to read behavioral cues, anticipating action, and approaching every subject with patience and respect, photographers can turn fleeting encounters into compelling stories.

In a recent development, the headphones, called MDR-3R, resemble the model that debuted with the first portable Walkman cassette player in 1979. However, the upcoming edition has a USB-C connector that works with most modern devices.

Other design news included Swedish designer Gustaf Westman’s unveiling of his full collection for media company Disney, including a bookstand shaped like Donald Duck and a mirror that resembles Pluto.

“Mickey’s ears and white gloves, Minnie’s bow, Goofy’s playful silhouette – they’re instantly recognisable shapes, and that made them really fun to work with,” Westman told Dezeen about working with the familiar characters.

American architect Steven Holl has designed a colourful watch for Swiss watch brand Cauny informed by a compliment architect Álvaro Siza once gave him, telling Holl he used colour “like Matisse”.

The colourful watch, which has a three-dimensional dial with red, green, yellow and blue colour blocks, was designed to be a dialogue between the two architects.

A housing development in Andorra designed by French studio Ateliers Jean Nouvel and Spanish studio Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos has been damaged in a fire.

Called La Querola, the project is shortlisted in the housing category of this year’s Dezeen Awards and recently won the awards’ public vote. The cause of the fire is unknown and no official estimate of the extent of the damage has been released so far.

In Shanghai, access to the staircase of the Grand Opera House by international studio Snøhetta has been restricted to ticket holders.

Sources indicate that access to the spiral staircase, which leads up to the roof and has become a popular spot for photos, now costs £5.60 per person. Snøhetta told Dezeen that “visitor management is necessary”.

In car news, Swedish brand Polestar has unveiled its Formula 2030 concept car that the brand notes “screams performance”.

The low-slung sports car has signature Dual Blade headlights and was intended to project power, with a long bonnet, wraparound windscreen, short overhangs, muscular haunches and 22-inch wheels.

In a roundup, we explored five examples of Mesoamerican modern architecture that combine principles from ancient architecture with modern techniques.

Curator and writer Su Wu chose five homes, which she indicates “reflect the complex aesthetic cultures of Mesoamerica”, from her book on the subject.

Popular projects on Dezeen this week include a former agricultural barn in Cornwall, a viewpoint informed by Viking rings and a playful Portuguese retreat.

Our podcast this week looked at the Cybertruck, asking: was it a flop or a design success?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recognizing a group show at a museum or nonprofit institution with a strong curatorial point of view or focused on a significant historical period.

“MONUMENTS”at The Geffen Contemporary at MOCA and The Brick, Los Angeles (October 23, 2025–May 3, 2026)Curators: Hamza Walker, Kara Walker, and Bennett Simpson, with Hannah Burstein and Paula Kroll.

Few exhibitions have the power to be decade-defining, but that is one way to describe “MONUMENTS.” A decade in the works, the show repositioned decommissioned Confederate monuments by placing them in spaces typically devoted to contemporary art. In MOCA’s galleries, the monuments were shown on the gallery floor as sculptural objects—many of them with graffiti still intact—rather than as elevated symbols of authority placed high above on pedestals, as they previously appeared in public settings. In showing the monuments this way, the show gave visitors a sense of what the statues’ true legacy means and how objects similar to them continue to shape US society. Related Articles ARTnews Awards 2026 Best Gallery Group Show: "Horror" ARTnews Introduces Nominees for Third Annual ARTnews Awards.

It has been revealed that with a sharp curatorial thesis that tackled a weighty concept, “MONUMENTS” also expertly placed these works in dialogue with the work of contemporary artists, including Bethany Collins, Julie Dash and Davóne Tines, Cauleen Smith, Torkwase Dyson, Andres Serrano, Martin Puryear, Nona Faustine, and Hank Willis Thomas, among others. Their varied stylistic approaches engaged with questions of monumentality, power, and who gets remembered in public spaces. At The Brick, cocurator Kara Walker presented Unmanned Drone (2023), for which she took apart a decommissioned equestrian statue of Stonewall Jackson and welded it back together in a fragmented way that acted as a metaphor for how we might piece together the fragments of history to create something newly introduced. Taken together, visitors could see how contemporary artists are essential in helping us navigate and process the unsettled debates around the toxic and pernicious histories that Confederate monuments embody.

Recent findings suggest that through these ambitious pairings, “MONUMENTS” displayed the unique capacity of art institutions to reframe history and bring it into productive friction with the present. A singular, once-in-a-generation exhibition, “MONUMENTS” is a study in what a thematic museum show can do.

Inaugural Hang of the David Geffen Galleriesat Los Angeles County Museum of ArtOpened May 4.

According to recent reports, while not a thematic exhibition in the traditional sense, the ARTnews Awards Jury felt that the hang that inaugurated LACMA’s David Geffen Galleries deserved a special commendation. LACMA’s at-times controversial building, designed by Peter Zumthor, presents a single floor spanning Wilshire Boulevard to hold the museum’s permanent collection. The aim was not to present one chronological narrative of art history but to think through how various eras, geographies, and styles can create commonalities when exhibited together. Key to the success of this hang was collaboration among the museum’s 15 curatorial departments. The curators’ work provides newly introduced insights into well-known works, spotlights lesser-known ones, and offers elegant juxtapositions.

“Into the Time Horizon”at the Nevada Museum of Art, Reno (November 15, 2025 – January 3, 2027)Curators: Apsara DiQuinzio, with Kolin Perry.

“If the word we: 59th Carnegie International”at the Carnegie Museum of Art, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania (May 2, 2026–January 3, 2027)Curators: Ryan Inouye, Danielle A. Jackson, and Liz Park.

“Let Us Gather in a Flourishing Way”at the Buffalo AKG Art Museum (March 6–September 6, 2026); traveled to Des Moines Art Center (October 24, 2026–January 24, 2027)Curator: Andrea Alvarez.

“Several Eternities in a Day: Form in the Age of Living Materials”at the Hammer Museum, Los Angeles (April 5, 2026–August 23, 2026)Curators: Pablo José Ramírez, with Jessi DiTillio.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two weeks after an abbreviated edition of Art Basel Paris, the 29th edition of Paris Photo has taken over the Grand Palais (until 15 November), where digital art is enjoying a moment in the spotlight.

The world of fine art photography is no stranger to controversies involving digital art, and it is heartening to witness the leading photography fair’s commitment to technological excursions within the medium. Featuring 12 exhibitors this year, the fourth iteration of Paris Photo’s digital sector has been curated by Marco De Mutiis of the Fotomuseum Winterthur, taking over from Nina Roehrs, who had helmed the first three editions.

Sources indicate that this year, the digital sector is accompanied by a pedagogical exhibition programme titled Soft Photography, organised by the École Cantonale d'Art de Lausanne in Switzerland and devoted to contextualising the place of AI and CGI within photography. Spanning an interactive exhibition and talks, Soft Photography aims to offer some much-needed dialogue between the medium’s analogue and digital wings.

Paris Photo 2026 at the Grand Palais in Paris © Grégoire Grange.

In a recent development, the digital sector certainly contains some AI-generated imagery, such as Fresh York- based Heft Gallery’s presentation of Alkan Avcıoğlu’s Disreality series, which is an expansion of the surreal landscape aesthetic he first introduced in a collaboration with Edward Burtynsky. But there are also plenty of analogue images throughout the sector, even photograms, enough to make one wonder just how much of a separate section this really is. A similar dynamic played out in the Zero 10 sector of Art Basel’s Swiss fair last June, where the term “digital art” was used so broadly that it begged the question whether a separate area was really warranted.

Noteworthy presentations at Paris Photo include the Venezuelan gallery Carmen Araujo Arte, which is showcasing Alejandro Cartagena’s mosaic-cut collages. Created from found photographs, the series is a manual interpretation of how images are made by generative AI by gathering found pixels. The works ask timely questions about authorship while also, in a rather sweet, analog gesture, highlighting just how much our art-making inevitably differs from that of algorithmic processes. The results are genuinely magnetic and intimate.

Palo Gallery’s installation of works from the artist duo Adrea Orejarena and Caleb Stein’s American Glitch series interrogates simulation theory as well as the nature of our screen-filled reality. Oscillating somewhere between the tone of David Lynch’s series Twin Peaks and surveillance footage, the presentation is a highlight, particularly Glitch Typologies (2020-24), the seven-channel sequence of floating images projected on the walls of a 3m-by-3m glass cube, the projectors hanging on a rod at its core, reminiscent of CCTV cameras. At a time of growing cultural cynicism, Orejarena and Stein offer a welcome reminder that the intersection of photography and technology can be whimsical, conspiratorial and surprising.

Yumo Wu, Old Dream No.1, 2026 Courtesy the artist and Licheng Ling Projects.

Yumo Wu’s solo stand with Licheng Ling Projects spans AI and darkroom analogue manipulation, with the images interspersed in such a manner that technique—though it inspires a certain sense of wonder—becomes secondary to the impact of the image. It is perhaps the best example at the fair of a presentation that moves beyond our fixation with what might be real and how it may have been created, with the artist instead asking her audience to quietly behold the images’ abstract textures. Wu is an emerging artist whose skill and willingness to experiment drowns out the noise, and the results are rather wonderful to behold. In addition to the stand marking her first solo presentation in Europe, one of her images is included in Paris Photo’s selection marking the bicentennial of the invention of photography.

Vincent Fournier, Orchis nubigena [Kunminga Gemina], 2026 Courtesy of the artist and Au Cube.

Industry observers note that vincent Fournier’s Flora Incognita, presented by Au Cube, features large-scale portraits of speculative flowers derived from existing flora and manipulated to depict what may happen to them on another planet, exposed to different kinds of radiation or gravity. The photos may at first register as AI-generated images, but were in fact created with CGI using Houdini, a comparatively old-school software. Each image is presented in a wooden frame with a golden plaque on the bottom featuring the name of the plant, evoking the kind of 18th- or 19th-century botanical illustration that particularly benefits from the aesthetics of the Grand Palais, whose architecture harks back to a time of earnest scientific fascination and discovery.

In a recent development, the New York gallery Nguyen-Wahed’s solo stand devoted to the Los Angeles-based photographer Summer Wagner contains unframed, romantic, large-scale photographs featuring grainy, densely-textured and coolly-lit portraits. The presentation, only digital insofar as the images were shot on a digital camera, deals with our relationship with reality as "we’ve collectively succumbed to the tsunami or cultural and technological changes that have thrown image-making into an existential crisis”, according to the artist.

Summer Wagner, Blue Shift, 2024 Courtesy of Nguyen Wahed and the artist.

Meanwhile, facing the digital sector is Ruttkowski 68’s solo stand devoted to François Hallard’s large-scale Polaroid prints of flowers, with the title “Conversations avec Claude” written by the artist in bold letters at the top of the booth. On the second day of previews, Hallard added “(Monet) not IA” to the title, after countless visitors had presumed the works were related to AI. Evidently Anthropic’s AI engine has eclipsed one of the most consequential painters of the 20th century—at least in its claim to the first name Claude.

Given how much of an impact the nascent field of AI-generated photography has had on photography at large, it is unsurprising that we continue to add disclaimers and coin terms to differentiate the medium’s analogue lineage from its technological step-cousins. Several years ago, the dealer Howard Greenberg told me he favours the term “lens-based” to differentiate the two, and this seemed adequate at the time. But since then, plenty of artists (myself included) have incorporated photographic lenses, enlargers and other analogue tools and processes to experiment with and human-wash digital imagery, so “lens-based” may no longer be up to the task of distinguishing between an image taken with a camera and an image generated with a computer. “Synthetic photography” does have a nice ring to it, although the word itself makes one think of things like latex and carcinogenic sunscreen. Perhaps “soft photography” is the best term, for the moment.

Paris Photo’s digital sector and the Soft Photography programming deftly and quietly tackle the discipline’s ongoing existential crisis by demonstrating that digital art predates many of the technologies we are debating today, and its applications in contemporary photography today are legion.

In 1982, Puerto Rican artist Papo Colo installed a book-shaped sculpture in the courtyard of El Museo del Barrio in Harlem. Commissioned as part of David Hammons’s Art in the Park program, it unfurled like an accordion across a series of 8-by-4-foot plywood panels co-authored by nearly 40 invited Newly introduced York artists and poets. Four decades later, seven of those panels form the basis of Octopus and Others, an exhibition that addresses the porous boundary between the word and the image within the more experimental scenes of production from the ‘80s through today.

The first panel in the exhibition is by Colo himself and gestures toward the alchemical, even transcendent possibilities unleashed through the collaboration of artists and poets across distances, languages, and generations. “English Spanish $ Spanglish,” Colo scribbles in white paint against the black-coated plywood. “Vivas poetas individuales X-formed by Colo’s ceremony into collective.”.

  • Schiller is the last surviving professional photographer to have worked with Monroe.
  • To mark the centennial of Monroe’s birth in 1926, The Latest York Historical will present Marilyn Monroe Centennial: Photographs by Lawrence Schiller, which will be on display from November 20, 2026, through March 28, 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An upcoming exhibition will feature photographs of Marilyn Monroe taken by Lawrence Schiller, the last living professional photographer to have worked with the Hollywood icon.

Schiller is the last surviving professional photographer to have worked with Monroe. He even saw the actress on the morning of August 4, 1962, the day she died at age 36, to discuss an upcoming photo shoot.

To mark the centennial of Monroe’s birth in 1926, The Latest York Historical will present Marilyn Monroe Centennial: Photographs by Lawrence Schiller, which will be on display from November 20, 2026, through March 28, 2027.

Although Monroe’s image has been reproduced countless times during her lifetime and in the decades since her death, the exhibition offers a closer look at how she managed her career and public image. Featuring 36 of Schiller’s photographs alongside his personal recollections, the exhibition explores Monroe’s efforts to shape how she was seen by the public.

The Latest York Historical’s photo exhibition juxtaposes the star’s on-camera and off-camera persona with images taken by photojournalist Schiller on two film sets, Let’s Make Love in 1960 and Monroe’s last and unfinished film Something’s Got to Give in 1962.

Recent findings suggest that while on assignment in Los Angeles for Look and Paris Match magazines, Schiller, then a young photographer, found Monroe to be a knowledgeable collaborator rather than simply a subject. Keenly aware of the power of imagery, Monroe showed Schiller how best to capture her.

“You’re already famous, now you’re going to make me famous,” Schiller mentioned to Marilyn in 1962 as he and Monroe discussed the photos he was about to take of her on the set of Something’s Got to Give.

“Don’t be so cocky,” Monroe replied, “photographers can be easily replaced.”.

It has been revealed that among the photographs on display is a series Schiller took during production of Something’s Got to Give. During a scene filmed on a closed set, Monroe spontaneously decided to remove the light nude-colored bikini bottoms she had been given and resurface naked. The resulting images, showing Monroe in the film’s swimming pool, appeared on magazine covers in more than 30 countries, including the cover of Life magazine.

Other photographs in the exhibition explore several defining aspects of Monroe’s 16-year, 30-film career in Hollywood. These include her efforts to be recognized as a serious actor, her relationships with acting coaches Lee and Paula Strasberg, and her attempts to gain greater control over her career. During her career, Monroe’s efforts to challenge the traditional studio system and become one of the first women in Hollywood to establish her own production organization.

Recent findings suggest that “Marilyn Monroe remains the definition of an icon, a sparkling presence on screen and a powerful storyteller in her own right who fought against the forces of her time,” Dr. Louise Mirrer, president and CEO of The Upcoming York Historical, notes in a statement. “While it’s true that Marilyn Monroe experienced great adversity and exploitation in her time, she also displayed remarkable resilience, sharp instincts, and physical mastery to ensure the camera captured her to her best advantage.

Dr Mirrer adds: “This exhibition attempts to showcase that agency through Lawrence Schiller’s exceptional photography, enlightening personal stories, and archival analysis drawn from our extensive collections.”.

More information about The New York Historical’s upcoming exhibition Marilyn Monroe Centennial: Photographs by Lawrence Schiller can be found here.
