📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recognized as the world’s most lucrative photography competition, the 15th annual HIPA awards celebrated its winners on November 10, 2026, with Family as this year’s theme. The awards were presented at the Museum of the Future, the torus-shaped architectural landmark in Dubai’s financial district in the United Arab Emirates. The 15th season has been a landmark for the Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum International Photography Award (HIPA). Over 1,000,000 photographs have been submitted, over 500,000 photographers have participated, and 209 countries have been represented cumulatively since the competition started in 2011.

This season featured five categories: Family, Portfolio (Story-Telling), Sports Photography, General (B&W and Color), and Dreams Through AI, which was a newly created category in response to public demand. Judge Tara Todras-Whitehill, an award-winning photojournalist from the US, quickly pointed out that it is better to keep AI-generated work in a separate category rather than have participants enter it in regular categories.

Recent findings suggest that the other notable judges were Ivan Pedretti, an Italian professional photographer; Kurt Mutchler, a former Senior Science Photo Editor at National Geographic; Germany’s Laci Perenyi, who has captured 21 Olympic Games; Sami Alramyan, a Kuwaiti documentary and humanitarian photographer for 20 years; American Santiago Lyon, Head of Advocacy and Education for the Adobe-led Content Authenticity Initiative; and Tomasz Tomaszewski, an acclaimed Polish photojournalist, with a Ph.D. from the Academy of Fine Arts in Warsaw.

His Highness Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum presented the $200,000 Grand Prize to photographer Pinu Rahman. His early-morning drone shot captured a family sleeping in their fire-devastated home, showing resilience and the human spirit.

Ali Bin Thalith, HIPA’s Secretary General, acknowledged the pivotal role of His Highness Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum in advancing the organization’s mission, recognizing his enduring commitment to promoting HIPA and fostering the global art of photography.

Here are the winning photos and videos of the 2026 competition, along with titles and descriptions submitted by the participating photographers.

Banker and amateur photographer Pinu Rehman bagged the Grand Prize for Under the Same Sky submitted to the Family category.

Industry observers note that on 25 November 2025, a large fire broke out at around 5:20 p.m. in Korail, one of Dhaka’s most densely populated informal settlements. Spreading rapidly through narrow lanes of tin, bamboo and wooden structures, the blaze destroyed approximately 1,500 homes and left thousands displaced. Photographed the following morning from above, a family of five sleeps side by side within the surviving concrete walls of their burned home. Around them lie twisted corrugated tin, charred debris, and the remains of neighboring shelters. A few salvaged belongings are gathered close. With their home gone, the family rests together in the only space still available to them.

The First Prize in Family went to Hamid Obaid Al Ali for The Promise of Tomorrow.

According to recent reports, captured during a macro dive, this rarely witnessed underwater moment indicates a tiny female sponge crab sheltering, her claws curled protectively around a dense cluster of developing eggs. The amber mass of eggs, each containing a life not yet emerged, rests against the textured surface of the sponge as the crab holds her position in the surrounding darkness. She will remain with her brood until the young are ready to enter the open ocean, where only a few will survive to adulthood. It is a reminder that parental devotion exists throughout the natural world, in places rarely seen.

The Second Prize was received by Nawaf Alosaimi for The Line.

A large herd of African elephants moves together across an open, darkened plain beneath a pale, cloud-streaked sky. A great matriarch leads from the front, her long tusks prominent and her wrinkled skin rendered in fine detail by the monochrome light. Younger elephants and calves press close among the adults, their trunks and legs forming a dense, overlapping mass of movement. Low hills and distant mountains sit along the horizon and a solitary elephant trails at the far edge of the frame, suggesting the full scale of the group crossing this vast, sweeping landscape.

The Third Prize went to Subhajit Datta for Framed Connection.

Sources indicate that A glass window on a cruise vessel in Ha Long Bay, Vietnam, becomes both mirror and membrane. A father’s reflection fills the frame, camera raised, while inside a mother and child sit together at a dining table, absorbed in a quiet moment. Beyond the glass, limestone karsts rise from the water and other vessels drift in the distance. Reflection, transparency and light combine interior and exterior into a single seamless image, holding three members of a family together within one composed and layered frame.

The First Prize was bagged by Filip Hrebenda for What the Earth Draws in Secret.

Seen from altitude, the landscape abandons all pretense of the familiar. Glacial channels thread across dark sediment in luminous arcs, their turquoise indifferent to the gravity that shaped them. Along a ridge between shadow and a burning yellow ground, bare trees stand in silhouette — neither quite rooted nor quite free, caught at the threshold between dormancy and something that resembles beginning. The photograph does not celebrate renewal so much as observe it in its raw, unfinished state: a world mid-sentence, still composing itself, legible only to those willing to look from far enough away.

Franco Banfi claimed the Second Prize for Give Me a Ride.

Recent findings suggest that A split-level view reveals an Olive Ridley sea turtle (Lepidochelys olivacea) resting at the surface of the open ocean while a Brown booby (Sula leucogaster) stands perched upon its olive-green shell. This well-documented yet unlikely relationship sees seabirds using surfacing turtles as floating platforms to roost and to feed on fish that gather beneath them. The turtle, protected as a vulnerable species, is the most abundant sea turtle in the Eastern Tropical Pacific. The arrangement offers a degree of mutual benefit: the booby gains a resting spot, while its presence may alert the turtle to approaching hazards.

Ramiro Torrents won Third Prize for Between Ice and Galaxies.

According to recent reports, at Laguna Torre, near El Chaltén in Patagonia, a rare convergence of conditions produced this panoramic night scene. The sky cleared completely, placing the arc of the Milky Way directly above the mountains, while soft moonlight shaped the landscape below. In a region notorious for violent weather, the wind dropped entirely, leaving the icebergs motionless on a still surface. The composition preserves the true scale and immense depth of the wilderness, holding a fleeting moment of absolute stillness in a landscape defined by change.

Taking home the First Prize honor was Jono Allen for Mahina and Mother.

Mahina, meaning “moon” in Tongan, is an albino humpback whale calf, a rarity estimated at one in 40,000. Her luminous white body rests close against her mother’s dark, barnacle-marked skin, the contrast between them striking and immediate. The two are at the start of a 4,000-mile migration to Antarctic waters, accompanied by a chosen male guardian. Active shipping lanes, ghost nets, killer whales, and great white sharks mark the route ahead. Mahina’s white coloring, visible from great distances, heightens the dangers. Her mother and guardian remain close, their protective instincts attuned to her exceptional vulnerability.

The Second-Place award went to Barun Sarkar for Beyond the Threads.

Recent findings suggest that three children peer through a curtain of tangled threads, their faces only partially visible behind the dense weave. Each face is held at a different depth—two side by side and one smaller figure below—their eyes directed outward with quiet intensity. The threads, loose and cascading, partially obscure yet cannot fully conceal the children’s gazes. The strands represent more than fabric: they stand for poverty, limited opportunity, and the barriers inherited across generations. Yet each pair of eyes remains fixed on what lies beyond, carrying hopes that the threads cannot contain.

The Third Prize was awarded to Thomas Vijayan for Black is Powerful.

According to recent reports, out of the quiet depth of night, a melanistic leopard moves forward along a lit track, wild grass bordering the path beside it. The animal emerges from near-total darkness, its pale eyes fixed and unwavering. Reflected light traces the outline of its form, revealing powerful musculature and the faint marks of old scars. The monochrome atmosphere deepens the contrast between the illuminated ground and the surrounding blackness, giving the scene a stillness that speaks to the leopard’s natural authority as one of nature’s most elusive predators.

The winner of the First Prize was Chi Hui Tang for Between Heaven and Earth.

A snow-covered mountain stands beneath a sweeping lenticular cloud formation, its grand form perfectly mirrored in a glass-still surface where mountain, cloud and sky dissolve into one another. A lone black horse gallops across the vast expanse; its small, dark form the only movement within an otherwise tranquil scene. The landscape exists as a dreamlike vision of absolute stillness, freedom and the enduring, elemental forces of nature.

The Second Prize category winner was Fan Ho Tsang for Dreams We Inherit.

Recent findings suggest that A high-speed train cuts through a tunnel of light, its sleek white form held sharp against streaks of blue and silver that radiate outward in every direction. The composition exaggerates the qualities of motion, light and perspective to carry the feeling of collective purpose—of generations moving forward together, each one building on the hopes and sacrifices of the last. The train becomes more than transport; it stands as a shared journey through time, carrying the weight of family and the inherited dreams they pass on.

The Third Prize was claimed by Bernardo Hernandez for Surfing the Sunset.

Along the beaches of Coveñas, Sucre, Colombia, a female surfer balances naturally atop a small breaking wave at sunset, warm light reflecting off the sea’s surface. The composition places the human figure in harmonious dialogue with the motion of the ocean, where the liquid textures of the water and the precision of the ride meet seamlessly within the warm, fading glow of the South American shoreline.

Yousef Alzanoon clinched the First Prize for Between Hunger and Fire.

Sources indicate that “The weight of war in Gaza unfolds in its most unsparing dimensions. Flares illuminate the city skyline at night, while buildings collapse in clouds of smoke and people move through rubble-strewn streets. Thousands gather around aid trucks, carrying sacks of flour across a landscape marked by destruction. Women press forward with empty cooking pots. Aid packages descend by parachute over coastal tent settlements, while families flee on horse-drawn carts carrying their remaining possessions. Mothers hold severely malnourished infants, and children bear the visible effects of acute starvation. The unfolding crisis bears witness to the profound scale of civilian suffering endured throughout the conflict.

The Second Prize was won by Brent Stirton for Rewilding Rhinos.

It has been revealed that “African Parks Network has assumed operational control of the world’s largest captive rhino breeding project, formerly owned by breeder John Hume, which houses over 2,000 southern white rhinos and more than 200 black rhinos. Following the operation’s bankruptcy, ownership was transferred to African Parks as a matter of urgency. The organization now faces the enormous challenge of translocating these animals to secure sites across Africa to bolster threatened populations, all while combating a relentless poaching epidemic. The narrative documents the scale and complexity of what may be the largest rewilding of an endangered species in history.

Don Pettit claimed the Third Prize for Milky Way from Orbit.

“These star-field time exposures were captured from the International Space Station using a customized, homemade sidereal star tracker. Rotating once every 90 minutes, the device counteracts the orbital motion of the ISS, allowing distant stars to be recorded as sharp, fixed points, something previously impossible in orbital photography. Across the expanse, Earth’s thin atmosphere glows with auroras in violet, crimson and gold, while city lights streak across the darkened surface below. The dense core of the Milky Way rises beyond the curve of the planet, with the structure of the ISS appearing in silhouette, a reminder of the human presence from which these views were made possible.

The First Place was won by Hongbin Wu for Winter Game.

“After heavy snowfall covered the mountainous Guoluo region of Qinghai, China, a group of young lamas cleared the basketball court at their temple and began an impromptu game. The concrete court forms a small island amid the surrounding snow, its dark surface contrasting with the vast white landscape. Dressed in scarlet robes, the young monks gather across the court, some playing while others watch from the edges. Their long shadows stretch across the ground beneath the winter sun. The quiet surroundings and lively game create a striking glimpse of youthful energy within the remote setting of monastic life.

The Second Place went to Faisal Hamada for Blazing Lap.

It has been revealed that “A McLaren Formula One car speeds across the circuit beneath a blazing sunset, its trajectory stretching the surrounding light into horizontal bands of amber, gold and deep black. The car appears small and sharply defined against the environment, while its papaya livery blends with the warm tones of the sky. Motion blur transforms the circuit and surrounding atmosphere into sweeping lines of color, emphasizing the speed of the passing car. Against the intensity of the sunset, the highly engineered machine becomes a fleeting silhouette, capturing a dramatic moment where precision, movement and light converge.

Third Place went to Kirill Kudryavtsev for Celestial Flare.

“During the men’s snowboard slopestyle qualification at the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympic Games in Livigno, Valtellina (Italy), Germany’s Noah Vicktor debuts into the alpine air above Livigno Snow Park. A luminous circular glow surrounds his airborne figure against a deep cobalt sky. The groomed slope cuts a sharp diagonal across the mountainscape, while Vicktor appears suspended at the center of the natural sun flare. The flare creates a striking contrast between the precision of the competition and the expansive mountain landscape, transforming a fleeting sporting moment into an almost celestial scene.

Véronique de Viguerie is a French photojournalist whose work explores the grey zones of a world too often portrayed in black and white. For more than twenty years, she has worked in conflict zones and societies marked by war, repression and political upheaval, from Afghanistan to Yemen, Iraq, Somalia, Nigeria, Syria and Mali. Yet war itself is not her subject. What interests her is what survives within it: desire, humor, beauty, absurdity, tenderness, resistance and the rhythms of ordinary life.

In a recent development, she does not photograph beauty in spite of war. She photographs beauty, desire, humor and color because they, too, are part of war. To exclude them would be to create another kind of distortion.

According to recent reports, this conviction has shaped her longstanding relationship with Afghanistan, which she first visited in 2003 and later lived in for four years. She has returned repeatedly to document Taliban fighters, civilians, women, families, and the profound transformation of Afghan society.

Her work on women has become increasingly central to this vision. De Viguerie is particularly interested in women living within restrictive or violent systems who are too often represented solely through what is done to them. Her photographs instead explore what they do: how they negotiate, resist, love, organize, protect and reinvent themselves, sometimes claiming power in spaces from which they have long been excluded.

Dr. Ali Mohamad is a photographer, documentary filmmaker, educator, and entrepreneur whose work is driven by a passion for visual storytelling and the creative industries. He founded TechMission, a digital media and production platform based in Dubai and serving the GC, alongside an education platform dedicated to empowering aspiring and professional photographers and videographers. Drawing on his industry experience, he shares practical knowledge that bridges technical expertise with creative vision, helping photographers and filmmakers refine their skills, develop their visual language, and approach their craft with greater confidence and purpose.

Kazuyoshi Nomachi (b. 1946) is an internationally acclaimed documentary photographer whose work explores the relationship between humanity, nature, and spirituality. Since his first journey to the Sahara in 1972, at age 25, he has devoted his career to documenting the lives, beliefs, and traditions of people inhabiting some of the world’s most challenging environments.

Industry observers note that his journey to the Sahara profoundly changed his direction. Moved by the strength of people living in its harsh environment, he turned to photojournalism and began a lifelong exploration of humanity’s relationship with the natural world.

In a recent development, inspired by the contrast between the Sahara’s aridity and the life-giving power of water, Nomachi began documenting the Nile in 1980. He traced the White Nile and followed the Blue Nile, capturing the extraordinary landscapes and communities shaped by these great rivers.

From 1988, Nomachi turned his attention to Asia. His work in western China introduced him to Tibet’s high-altitude communities and the spiritual traditions of Tibetan Buddhism. Between 2004 and 2008, he explored the sacred origins of the Ganges, documenting the landscapes and traditions central to Hinduism.

From 1995 to 2000, Nomachi photographed the holy cities of Mecca and Medina in Saudi Arabia, documenting the Hajj pilgrimage and the profound devotion of Muslims gathering in Mecca. Beginning in 2002, he explored the Andean highlands of Peru and Bolivia, examining the blending of Catholicism and Inca cultural traditions, a project he has continued to pursue.

Among his many honors are the Photographic Society of Japan’s Annual Award, received in 1990 and 1997, and Japan’s Medal of Honor with Purple Ribbon, awarded in 2009.

Framed by their car’s windshield, and then again by my rearview mirror, a man and a woman who seem to be a couple look like they'd rather be anywhere but together. He’s behind the wheel, doing all the talking; she’s looking straight ahead, motionless like a marble statue. Gradually, her face wears a desperate expression that only grows more hopeless as he continues talking and gesticulating.

In the supermarket checkout line, I pick up a copy of TIME magazine for the first time in God knows how long, drawn to a painting of Jesus Christ on the cover. It’s a special edition promising to tell us “Who he was. Who he is. His miracles, his mission, his love.” I expect to see a lot of biblical sheep inside, but I don’t find any. I buy the matter as an artifact. I stopped believing in TIME magazine a long time ago.

GR gallery is pleased to present My Screen Tests, the first New York City solo exhibition by Kohei Yamada. The exhibition examines the enduring value of the authentic relationship between artist and artwork, engaging in themes of irony, introspection, and visual metaphor, which draw inspiration from contemporary practice and Yamada’s nuanced admiration for American Pop art.

Sources indicate that presenting a new suite of paintings on canvas -each paired with its esquisse on paper- In My Screen Tests, Yamada searches within New York City’s identity as the art capital of the world in order to infuse his work with a distinct vitality, revealing his admiration for Andy Warhol through motifs referencing the Silver Factory era and its entourage, and evoking tension between a sense of historical prestige and vibrant pop expressions. This interplay initiates a critical conversation between perceptions of art and is worthwhile in examining the creative directions of today’s world.

My Screen Tests is defined by motivations that comment on the ambiguous nature of art’s true value beyond its creator, while also alluding to Yamada’s need to remain bound to art for the rest of his life. The work also critiques the world’s normalization of deceit and capitalistic greed, alongside a persistent.

Recent findings suggest that longing for freedom that remains just out of reach. Fresh York City lies at the core of Yamada’s practice, serving as both subject and catalyst for exploring the interplay between personal perception and nostalgia. It also functions as a cultural bridge between American and Japanese influences, tracing the artist’s journey from childhood through his engagement with the legacy of Andy Warhol, as well as other Japanese and American artists. Through a combination of brushwork, abstraction, and figuration, Yamada weaves a narrative rich in contemporary art history, while also confronting the true value of an artist’s existence.

Over half of the works exclusively made for My Screen Tests are imbued with references inspired by Warhol’s practice and artistic values, cast against Newly introduced York City as a hub for experimentation where art meets and even challenges commerce. Repetition and humor are also at the core of the artist’s creative process, adding a wittiness and discipline to his work, while also connecting it on a deeper level to the Pop tradition. Yamada draws upon the city as both muse and stage, invoking a range of artistic influences as main characters, while ultimately revealing each to be a projection of his own identity.

Industry News: After a year off, the ADAA's New York fair returns with a new name and revamped layout

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Since 1989, the Art Dealers Association of America (ADAA) had hosted its Art Show, which brought member galleries from across the country together for an annual fair in New York.
  • Sources indicate that this week, the newly-renamed ADAA Fair returns to the Park Avenue Armory (until 16 November), the first solely under the leadership of Kinsey Robb, who joined in 2024.
  • Sources indicate that “It’s a continuation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since 1989, the Art Dealers Association of America (ADAA) had hosted its Art Show, which brought member galleries from across the country together for an annual fair in New York. Last year, the ADAA cancelled the 2025 fair less than four months before it was set to open, citing a need to take a “strategic pause” to reevaluate how to best serve its members.

Sources indicate that this week, the newly-renamed ADAA Fair returns to the Park Avenue Armory (until 16 November), the first solely under the leadership of Kinsey Robb, who joined in 2024. Despite the latest name and a few tweaks, it remains the same fair, she notes.

Sources indicate that “It’s a continuation. It's an evolution,” Robb indicates. “It is still a small-scale collegial fair of the members, so that hasn't changed either. It's just adapting into the environment and the time that we're in.”.

One of those new aspects is a smaller exhibitor list. This year, 63 galleries are participating, around 12 fewer than the last edition. The intention was to give the fair more focus in a time when dealers and collectors alike are complaining of "fairtigue", both due to frequency and size (Art Basel Miami Beach, the largest art fair in the Western Hemisphere, will also scale down participating galleries this year).

The hiatus “gave us an opportunity to look at the oversaturation of fairs that were happening at that time, and the fatigue that people were feeling,” Kinsey states. “This scale feels nice to me.”.

The reduction allows for a larger space around the circular bar at the center of this year’s fair, affording attendees more space to move and cut through the three-aisle expo. Visitors naturally found themselves socialising at the centre of the fair during the opening gala for the Whitney Museum of American Art on Thursday (12 November), which was well-attended despite the stormy weather and even a tornado warning in New York City. (During the ADAA fair's hiatus, its longtime preview night partner and beneficiary, the Henry Street Settlement, teamed up with the Independent fair.).

The partnership with the Whitney Museum has brought in a upcoming, often-younger crowd, participating dealers say; works on display, meanwhile, skew heavily toward Modern and post-war secondary-market material rather contemporary works.

“I think deeply about the ecosystem of the art world, and how we all are connected,” Kinsey indicates. “Even if we all are in our own lanes or bubbles, we are all essential to each other in service of the art and in service of the artist.”.

The dealers participating range from stalwarts like Hirschl & Adler and Kraushaar Galleries, founding members of the ADAA who participated in the Art Show’s inaugural edition in 1989, to first-time exhibitors like Alexander Berggruen, Sargent's Daughters, Piero Atchugarry, Nicodim and Hollis Taggart.

Industry observers note that taggart has run his namesake gallery for nearly 50 years but only recently became an ADAA member, he says, allowing him to apply for and participate in the fair for the first time. He says that in the first few hours of the opening gala, he saw a great crowd of visitors, often from the surrounding Upper East Side, different from the crowd that comes to the openings in Chelsea, where he has a space. The gallery is presenting a dual stand dedicated to two women Abstract Expressionist painters: Michael (Corinne) West and Teruko Yokoi.

Industry observers note that “I think it's very mixed, it’s a bifurcated market,” Taggart says of the art market leading up to the fair. “There’s so many daily events that happen politically and financially, like the meltdown with Nvidia. I think the market's OK, but when you consider world events, it's a miracle that it's still as good as it is.”.

The most valuable transactions reported to date at the fair are Agnes Pelton’s The Well of Peace (1932), which had an asking price of $2.4m, and Beauford Delaney’s Untitled (Paris) (1986), which was priced at $1.6m, both from the stand of Fresh York-based dealer Jonathan Boos.

Sources indicate that another Upper East Side local, Kraushaar Galleries, reported the sale of two paintings for six-figure sums, as well as several works priced below $2,000. James Barron Art says it sold works by Beverly Pepper, Kenneth Noland and Kikuo Saito, each priced between $40,000 and $85,000, while Yoshii Gallery sold several works priced between $6,000 and $80,000. The Chelsea-based gallery and advisory firm AH Arts sold a work on paper by Helen Frankenthaler for $75,000. The international gallery Perrotin sold out of works by Susumu Kamijo, whose paintings on the stand were priced between $30,000 and 45,000. Jessica Silverman from San Francisco reported eight sales from its presentation of new works by Julie Buffalohead, ranging in price from $22,000 and $50,000.

According to recent reports, the Tribeca-based dealer Charles Moffett, who previously took part in the 2024 edition, says he appreciated the 2025 break and how the ADAA doesn’t pressure members to take part. During the opening gala, Moffett’s gallery sold four paintings by Lily Stockman priced at $20,000 apiece, and three paintings by Julia Jo priced at $30,000 each.

Sources indicate that “With so many of the fairs, once you're on the hamster wheel, it's like, go go go. You apply every year, and if you don't apply or if you decide to sit out a year, you go to the back of the line,” Moffett says. “I'm just grateful that this feels more like an organisation that wants to see the best for each gallery.”.
